title: Sorting materials: how the rule you choose decides the groups

summary.text: Ask 'Is it hard?', and a steel spoon and a wooden spoon go in the same group. Ask 'Is it shiny?', and they go in different groups. Sorting means putting things into groups by a rule, and the rule decides the groups. The child sorts one heap in several ways, and settles tricky things, like a candle, with a test. They also learn three sorting tools: the Venn diagram, the Carroll table and the branching key. Scientists sorted elements, stars and living things in the same way, and some of those sorts led to discoveries.
summary.art: A heap of everyday things (a steel spoon, a wooden spoon, a glass bangle, a rubber band, a candle) with three arrows leading to three different pairs of piles, each pile pair labelled with a different question mark.

intro.hook: Try this. Put six things on the floor: a steel spoon, a wooden spoon, a glass bangle, a rubber band, a comb and a candle. Make two groups. Now mix them up and make two different groups. How many different ways can you find?
intro.text: In every town in India there is a kabadiwala. This is a person who buys old newspapers, bottles, tins and iron. He or she sells them on, so they can be made into new things. Watch a kabadiwala work and you see sorting all day long. Paper goes here. Glass goes there. Iron goes in a third pile. But the same heap could be sorted in many other ways: by colour, by weight, or by whether it rings when you drop it. Which way is right? That depends on what the sorting is for.
intro.art: A kabadiwala sitting beside a weighing scale, with neat piles of newspaper, bottles, tins and iron around him, and a child watching and holding up a bottle.

outcomes: I can sort a set of things into groups using a rule, and say what the rule is.
I can sort the same things in more than one way. I can say why one thing lands in different groups.
I can deal with a tricky thing that does not fit. I can make the rule clearer, add a middle group or use a test.
I can sort by two rules at once, using a Venn diagram and a Carroll table.
I can build and use a branching key made of yes or no questions. I can say which key is fastest.
I can give examples of how people sort in real life, like kabadiwalas and recycling plants. I can say why the rule must fit the job.
I can tell how sorting led to big discoveries, such as the periodic table and the types of stars.
I can say what scientists still argue about when they sort, such as species, Pluto and sand. I can say why the rule we choose matters.

terms.meaning: To put things into groups, using a rule.
terms.example: Putting the spoons in one drawer and the cups in another is sorting.
terms.art: A child dropping spoons into one box and cups into another.

terms.meaning: A set of things that fit the same rule.
terms.example: All the wooden things in your kitchen are one group.
terms.art: A ring drawn round three wooden things.

terms.meaning: The question you ask about every thing, to decide which group it goes in. A good rule has a clear yes or no answer.
terms.example: 'Is it shiny?' is a rule. Every thing is either shiny or it is not.
terms.art: A card with a question mark, held over two boxes marked Yes and No.

terms.meaning: What a thing is made of, such as wood, metal, glass or rubber.
terms.example: A steel spoon is made of the material steel.
terms.art: A spoon with a label arrow pointing to the word steel.

terms.meaning: Something you can find out about a material by looking, touching or testing. Hard, soft, shiny, dull and bendy are properties.
terms.example: Glass is hard and see-through. Cotton is soft and bendy.
terms.art: A hand pressing on a glass bangle and a cotton cloth.

terms.meaning: A thing that is hard to place, because it is between two groups or fits both.
terms.example: A candle feels hard, but a fingernail can scratch it. Is it hard or soft?
terms.art: A candle sitting on the line between a Hard box and a Soft box.

terms.meaning: In a sort with two rules, a thing can fit both rules, or fit neither.
terms.example: A steel spoon is both shiny and hard. A woollen sock is neither.
terms.art: Two overlapping circles with a spoon in the middle and a sock outside.

terms.meaning: A drawing of overlapping circles. Each circle is one rule. Things that fit both rules go where the circles overlap.
terms.example: One circle for shiny, one for hard. The spoon goes in the overlap.
terms.art: Two overlapping circles labelled Shiny and Hard, with a spoon in the overlap.

terms.meaning: A table that sorts things by two yes or no rules. It is also called a Carroll diagram. It has four boxes: yes and yes, yes and no, no and yes, no and no.
terms.example: The boxes are shiny and hard, shiny and soft, dull and hard, dull and soft.
terms.art: A four-box table with a small drawing in each box.

terms.meaning: A question that can only be answered with yes or no. Good sorting uses these.
terms.example: 'Is it made of metal?' can be answered yes or no.
terms.art: A speech bubble with a question, and two buttons, Yes and No.

terms.meaning: A chart of yes or no questions that finds one thing from a group, step by step. It looks like a tree turned on its side.
terms.example: A key for a brick, ice, a balloon and paper asks 'Is it hard?' Yes. Then 'Is it shiny?' No. So it is the brick.
terms.art: A tree-shaped chart: one question splitting into two, then two more, ending in four small drawings.

terms.meaning: A way of counting by making one mark for each thing. The fifth mark crosses the first four.
terms.example: Four marks and a line across make five.
terms.art: Tally marks in groups of five beside a pile of spoons.

terms.meaning: Something you do to a thing to find out the answer to a rule, instead of guessing.
terms.example: To test hard or soft, press a fingernail into it.
terms.art: A thumbnail pressing into a candle.

terms.meaning: Three groups for the state of a material. A solid keeps its shape. A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container. A gas spreads out to fill all the space it can.
terms.example: A stone is a solid. Water is a liquid. Steam is a gas.
terms.art: A stone, a glass of water and a kettle with steam, each in its own circle.

terms.meaning: Materials that do not fit neatly into solid or liquid, such as jelly, toothpaste, foam and wet cornflour. Scientists give them their own group.
terms.example: Toothpaste stays on the brush like a solid, but squeezes out like a liquid.
terms.art: A tube of toothpaste with a curl of paste sitting on a toothbrush.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
terms.example: A steel spoon has more atoms in it than you could ever count.
terms.art: A spoon, then a zoom to a speck, then a cluster of tiny balls.

terms.meaning: One kind of atom, such as iron, carbon, oxygen or gold. Scientists know 118 elements, and every material is made from them.
terms.example: Iron is an element. Steel is made of iron and a little carbon.
terms.art: A row of small boxes, each holding one coloured ball, labelled iron, carbon, gold.

terms.meaning: A chart that sorts all the elements into rows and columns. Elements that behave alike sit in the same column.
terms.example: Gold, silver and copper sit in the same column, and all are shiny metals.
terms.art: A grid of coloured squares with a few squares circled in one column.

terms.meaning: A group that astronomers use to sort stars by their light. The type tells how hot the surface of the star is, and it matches the star's colour.
terms.example: The Sun is a yellow star. Betelgeuse is a red star.
terms.art: A line of stars from blue on the left to red on the right.

terms.meaning: One kind of living thing, such as a tiger, a banyan tree or a human. Biologists argue about the best way to say exactly what a species is.
terms.example: A tiger and a lion are two different species.
terms.art: A tiger and a lion standing side by side with a question mark between them.

terms.meaning: A big, careful system of groups inside groups, made by experts. Scientists classify animals, plants, stars and elements.
terms.example: Cats belong to the group mammals, which belongs to the group animals.
terms.art: Nested circles: cat inside mammals inside animals.

terms.meaning: A person who buys old paper, bottles, tins and metal, sorts them into piles, and sells them to be recycled.
terms.example: The kabadiwala weighs your old newspapers and pays you for them.
terms.art: A man with a hand-held scale weighing a bundle of newspapers.

terms.meaning: Turning old things into new things by melting, shredding or pulping them. Recycling works much better when the materials are sorted first.
terms.example: Old glass bottles are melted and made into new bottles.
terms.art: A pile of bottles going into a furnace and coming out as new bottles.

terms.meaning: Sorting grain from husk by tossing it in a flat basket so the wind carries the light husk away.
terms.example: A farmer tosses rice in a sup, and the husk blows off.
terms.art: A woman tossing grain from a flat basket, husk drifting sideways and grain falling straight down.

terms.meaning: A solid whose atoms are in an ordered pattern that never repeats. Scientists once thought such a thing was impossible. Then one was found.
terms.example: A quasicrystal was found inside a meteorite from space.
terms.art: A shape made of tiles that makes a five-pointed pattern but never repeats.

explanations.definition: Sorting is putting things into groups, using a rule. The rule is a question that every thing can answer.
explanations.description: Pour a bag of things onto the floor. There is a steel spoon, a wooden spoon, a rubber band and a pebble. To sort them, pick a rule such as 'Is it made of wood?'. Each thing goes in the yes group or the no group. Every sort has three parts. There are the things, the rule and the groups. The things stay the same. If you change the rule, the groups change. Sorting is one of the oldest tools of thinking. It helps us find things, count things and see patterns.
examples: Putting spoons in one drawer and cups in another.
Putting clothes into piles for the dhobi: whites, colours and woollens.
A school library putting all the story books on one shelf and all the science books on another.
explanations.art: A heap of things on a floor, a question-mark card, and two boxes labelled Yes and No with the things divided between them.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what sorting is, and what its three parts are.

explanations.definition: The group a thing goes in depends on the rule we use. The same thing can go in different groups under different rules.
explanations.description: The same things can be sorted in many ways. Which group a thing lands in depends on the rule, not only on the thing. Take a brick. Sort by hard or soft, and the brick goes in the hard group. Sort by shiny or dull, and the very same brick goes in the dull group. The brick did not change. Only the question changed. This is why scientists always say what rule they used. 'This is the hard group' means nothing unless we say what hard means. The table shows one set of six things sorted in three different ways.
examples: A steel spoon is in the shiny group, the hard group and the metal group, all at once.
A woollen sock is in the soft group, the dull group and the bendy group.
A glass bangle is in the hard group and the see-through group, but not in the bendy group.
explanations.art: The same six objects shown three times, each time with a different pair of rings around them.
explanations.context: Have you noticed that one thing can belong to many groups? This card shows the same six things sorted three different ways.

chart.title: The same six things, sorted three ways (a made-up example)

explanations.definition: A good rule is a yes or no question. It gives the same answer for everyone, because it can be checked by looking or by a test.
explanations.description: A good rule has a clear answer, and the answer is the same whoever asks. 'Is it shiny?' is a good rule. You can look and decide. 'Is it pretty?' is not. Your friend may disagree. 'Is it heavy?' is not good either, because heavy for a baby is light for a wrestler. A better rule is 'Is it heavier than a 1 kilogram packet of atta?'. For rules like hard and soft, we can use a test. If a fingernail leaves a mark, we call it soft. Then we use the same test on every thing, in the same way. That makes the sort fair.
examples: 'Is it made of metal?' is a good rule. 'Is it nice?' is not.
'Does a fingernail scratch it?' gives the same answer for you and your cousin.
'Is it big?' is a poor rule until we say 'Is it longer than a hand?'.
explanations.art: Two question cards: 'Is it shiny?' with a tick, and 'Is it pretty?' with a cross and two children arguing.
explanations.context: Not every question works for sorting. This card explains what a good sorting rule looks like.

explanations.definition: A tricky middle is a thing that does not clearly belong to one group. We can fix it with a sharper rule, a middle group or a test.
explanations.description: Some things will not fit. A candle feels hard, but a fingernail can scratch it. A plastic cup is stiff, but it bends a little. Sand pours like water, yet each grain is hard. These things sit in the tricky middle. Finding one is not a mistake. It shows you exactly where the rule is unclear. There are three things you can do. First, make the rule sharper, so it says exactly what counts. Second, add a middle group. Third, use a test, and let the test decide. Sometimes a tricky thing shows that the rule needs to change.
examples: A candle: add a middle group called 'hard but scratchable', or use the fingernail test.
A plastic cup: ask 'Does it bend when I press it with my thumb?'. Then the answer is clear.
A foil ball: shiny on the outside, but crumpled and dull in the dents.
explanations.art: A candle on the line between a Hard box and a Soft box, with a child holding a fingernail over it.
explanations.context: This card is about things that do not fit neatly in any group, and what to do about them.

explanations.concept: Two rules at once: Venn and Carroll
explanations.definition: A Venn diagram and a Carroll table both sort things by two rules at once. Each shows things that fit both, one, or neither.
explanations.description: Sometimes one rule is not enough. A Venn diagram uses two overlapping circles, one for each rule. Things that fit both rules go in the overlap. Things that fit only one go in that circle alone. Things that fit neither go outside both circles. A Carroll table, also called a Carroll diagram, does the same job with four boxes. Its columns say yes or no to the first rule. Its rows say yes or no to the second. Both tools show four kinds of thing: both, only the first, only the second and neither. The Venn diagram is named after John Venn, an English thinker who used it in the 1880s. The Carroll table is named after Lewis Carroll, the author of Alice in Wonderland, who was also a maths teacher. He loved puzzles that sort things with logic.
examples: Shiny circle and hard circle. A steel spoon goes in the overlap. A wooden spoon goes in 'hard' only. A foil ball goes in 'shiny' only. A woollen sock goes outside both.
In a Carroll table, the same spoon goes in the box 'shiny and hard'.
explanations.art: A Venn diagram of two circles on the floor with objects placed, and next to it a four-box table with the same objects.
explanations.context: Here you will learn two tools for sorting by two rules at once.

chart.title: A Carroll table for four things (a made-up example)

explanations.definition: A branching key is a chart of yes or no questions. It sorts a group step by step until each thing is alone.
explanations.description: A branching key finds one thing in a group by asking yes or no questions, one after another. Each question splits the group into two smaller groups. Ask a new question for each smaller group. Keep going until each thing is alone at the end of a branch. Try it with four things: a brick, ice, a balloon and paper. 'Is it hard?' Brick and ice say yes. Balloon and paper say no. Next, 'Is it shiny?' separates the brick from the ice. 'Is it waterproof?' separates the balloon from the paper. If every question splits its group in half, each question doubles the number of branches. One question gives two. Two give four. Three give eight. So eight things can be found with just three good questions. A key that picks out only one thing with each question can need seven.
examples: A key to find which of four fruits you are holding.
A doctor's chart that asks yes or no questions to work out an illness.
A bird book key: 'Does it have a long beak?' Yes, go to question 4.
explanations.art: A tree chart on its side: one starting question, two branches, two more questions, ending in four small drawings of a brick, ice, a balloon and paper.
explanations.context: This card explains the branching key, a very handy sorting tool that works like the game of Twenty Questions.

chart.title: How the number of branches grows with each question

explanations.definition: The rules used for sorting materials come in families. They sort by material, property, use, origin or state.
explanations.description: People use some kinds of rules again and again. One family sorts by what a thing is made of, such as wood, metal or glass. Another family sorts by properties, such as hard or soft, shiny or dull, bendy or stiff. A third sorts by use, such as things for cooking, writing or building. A fourth sorts by where a thing came from, such as natural things or made things. A fifth sorts by state, such as solid, liquid or gas. Some rules need a tool. A magnet attracts iron and most kinds of steel, but not aluminium or copper, so it can sort them apart. Here we practise the skill that they all share. We choose a rule, apply it fairly, and see what the groups tell us.
examples: By material: all the steel things in the kitchen.
By property: everything that is see-through.
By use: everything we eat with.
By origin: things from plants, things from animals, things from factories.
explanations.art: Five signposts pointing in five directions, labelled made of, like, used for, came from, and state.
explanations.context: There are many kinds of sorting rules. This card gives a map of the main families, so you can pick one on purpose.

explanations.concept: Sorting a heap for real: people and machines
explanations.definition: Real sorting uses rules that match the job. Hands, wind, magnets and cameras are all tools for applying a rule.
explanations.description: A kabadiwala sorts by hand and by eye. Paper goes to one pile. Bottles go to another. Iron goes in a third. Why? Each material is recycled in its own way, so each pile can be sold to a different buyer. Farmers sort too. To winnow grain, they toss it in a flat basket called a sup. The heavier grain falls back down. The lighter husk blows away. The wind sorts light from heavy. A modern recycling plant sorts in layers. First, big magnets attract and lift out iron and steel. Next, a machine uses a changing magnetic field to make aluminium cans jump out of the stream. Then cameras that see invisible light recognise different plastics. Little jets of air blow each kind into its own bin. In India, a great deal of recycling still begins with waste pickers, who sort by hand. Many of them are women. They can tell many kinds of plastic, paper and metal apart by look, feel and sound.
examples: A kabadiwala sorting by hand into paper, plastic, glass and metal.
A farmer winnowing rice in a sup.
A recycling plant using magnets, cameras and air jets.
A cook picking stones out of dal before cooking.
explanations.art: A conveyor belt with a magnet lifting tins, a camera above it and little air jets blowing plastic bottles into bins, with a waste picker sorting by hand beside it.
explanations.context: People and machines sort heaps all day. This card shows how, and why each sort uses the rule it does.

explanations.concept: Solid, liquid, gas: a rule with a fuzzy edge
explanations.description: Sorting by state seems easy. A solid keeps its shape. A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container. A gas spreads out to fill all the space it can. But many things will not stay in one group. Rice pours like a liquid, but every grain is a hard solid. Toothpaste is a solid on your brush and a liquid when squeezed. Wet cornflour, called oobleck, flows when you move it slowly. It turns hard when you punch it. Ketchup stays put in a bottle, then runs when you shake it. Scientists did not ignore these. They gave them a new group, called soft matter, and now study them closely. Scientists also added more states. Plasma is a glowing gas in which atoms are torn apart. It makes up lightning, neon signs and the Sun. And when some atoms are cooled to almost the coldest temperature possible, they form another state, the Bose-Einstein condensate. It is named after Satyendra Nath Bose, from Kolkata, and Albert Einstein, who predicted it in 1924 and 1925. It was first made in a laboratory in 1995. The full story of how a pile of grains flows is still being worked out.
examples: Rice and sand: grains that flow like a liquid.
Jelly, toothpaste, foam: soft matter.
Lightning and the Sun: plasma.

perspectives.explanation: Everything is a solid, a liquid or a gas. Rice is just many small solids. Sorting is simple if you ask what each grain is doing, not the whole pile.

Many everyday materials behave in between. They do not fit three groups, so a new group is needed. A famous 1996 paper by Heinrich Jaeger, Sidney Nagel and Robert Behringer was named 'Granular solids, liquids, and gases'. A pile of grains can act like any of the three.

At the atom level, the groups are about how free the atoms are. In a solid they jiggle in place. In a liquid they slide past each other. In a gas they fly about. The edge between them is real, but it can be blurry.

explanations.art: A kitchen shelf with rice, ketchup, toothpaste and jelly each sitting on a line between a stone and a glass of water.
explanations.context: You might think sorting into solid, liquid and gas is easy. This card is about the things that will not stay in one group.

explanations.definition: The periodic table sorts the elements by how they behave and by their weight. Gaps in it led to the discovery of new elements.
explanations.description: Everything you can touch is made of atoms. There are only about 118 kinds, called elements. Iron is an element. So are carbon, oxygen, gold and helium. About ninety of them are found in nature. In 1869, 63 elements were known. A Russian chemist, Dmitri Mendeleev, sorted them by the weight of their atoms, and also by how they behave. Elements that behaved alike, such as the soft metals that fizz in water, kept turning up in the same column. His table worked, but not perfectly. In some places, no known element fitted the pattern. Mendeleev did something brave. He left those places empty and said that undiscovered elements would fill them. He even wrote what these elements would be like. Between 1875 and 1886, three of them were found: gallium, scandium and germanium. Their properties were close to what he had written. A good sort does more than tidy. It lets you guess what you have not found yet. Others had seen parts of the pattern before. John Newlands, in England, arranged elements in 1865 and was laughed at. One chemist asked him if he had tried listing them in alphabetical order. In 1887 he was given a medal for his discovery.
examples: Mendeleev left a gap and predicted an element he called eka-silicon. In 1886 it was found and named germanium.
Marguerite Perey, a French scientist who worked with Marie Curie's team, found the element francium in 1939. It filled one of the last empty places in the table.
explanations.art: A big grid of cards on a table with a few empty squares, and a hand holding a card that fits into one gap.
explanations.context: Scientists sorted all the kinds of atoms into one big chart. This card tells how, and how the sort let them predict new elements.

explanations.definition: Elements in the same column of the periodic table have the same kind of outer electrons. That is why they behave alike.
explanations.description: Why do elements in the same column behave alike? The answer is hidden inside the atom. Every atom has tiny electrons around its edge. The outer electrons decide how an atom joins with others. Elements in the same column have the same number of outer electrons, or a very similar arrangement. So they act alike. Mendeleev did not know any of this. He found the pattern before anyone knew the reason. Later, in 1913, an English scientist named Henry Moseley used X-rays to find a whole number for each element, its atomic number. It counts the protons in the middle of the atom. Sorting by that number put the table in perfect order. Moseley died at 27, in the First World War. Many scientists think this was one of the greatest losses to science. So Mendeleev's sort, made only from how elements behave, turned out to follow the inside of the atom.
examples: Sodium and potassium both fizz in water. They sit in the same column and each has one outer electron.
Neon, argon and helium hardly join with anything. They sit in the last column, with their outer electrons full.
explanations.art: Three atoms drawn as a nucleus with rings of electrons, the outer ring highlighted, sitting in a column.
explanations.context: Mendeleev sorted the elements by how they behave, without knowing why his sort worked. This card goes inside the atom to find the reason.

explanations.definition: Astronomers sort stars into types by their light: O, B, A, F, G, K and M. The types show how hot the star's surface is, from blue-white and hottest to red and coolest.
explanations.description: Look at the night sky. Stars are not all the same colour. Some are blue-white, some yellow, some orange and some red. From the 1880s, a team of women at the Harvard College Observatory in America sorted photographs of starlight. Each photograph spread a star's light into a thin rainbow crossed by dark lines. Williamina Fleming began as a maid in the director's home. He saw how clever she was and hired her, and she became one of the observatory's best star sorters. Annie Jump Cannon carried the work on. She lost much of her hearing as a young woman, and she worked for over forty years. She sorted about 350,000 stars by the pattern of lines in their light. At her best she could place three stars in a minute. She put the star types in the order of seven letters, O B A F G K M. Her order also ran from blue-white stars to red ones. It became the world's standard. The Sun is a G star. But what did the letters mean? In 1925 a young scientist, Cecilia Payne, showed that the types are really about temperature. She used a theory made in 1920 by an Indian scientist, Meghnad Saha. She also showed that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium. A senior astronomer, Henry Norris Russell, told her this could not be right, so she wrote that it was probably not real. In 1929 he reached the same answer himself. Sorting starlight had uncovered what the stars are made of.
examples: Rigel, in the Orion constellation, is a blue-white B star. Betelgeuse, in the same constellation, is a red M star.
The Sun is a yellow G star, with a surface at about 5,500 degrees Celsius.
explanations.art: A long table with women in long dresses sorting glass photographs of star light, and a tall chart on the wall showing stars from blue to red.
explanations.context: Sorting also works on things far away. This card is about how women at an observatory sorted the light of stars, and found out what stars are.

chart.title: The star types, from hottest to coolest

explanations.concept: Sorting living things: where does the platypus go?
explanations.description: Living things need sorting too. In the 1700s, a Swedish scientist, Carl Linnaeus, sorted plants and animals into groups inside groups. At first people sorted by looks. Whales were put with fish, because they live in water and have fins. But a whale breathes air and feeds its babies on milk. So whales belong with mammals. DNA shows that the whale's closest living relative is the hippo. Then came the platypus, an animal in Australia with fur and a duck-like bill, which lays eggs. In 1799 a British scientist, George Shaw, described a platypus skin sent from Australia. He wrote that it was hard to believe it was real, and he is said to have looked for stitches. But the platypus is real. It is a mammal that lays eggs. Biologists still argue about the most basic group of all, the species. They have written more than twenty different definitions. A tomato is a puzzle too. To a botanist it is a fruit. To a cook it is a vegetable. In 1893, the highest court in America decided that, for a tax on vegetables, a tomato counts as a vegetable. Each person used the rule that fit their job.
examples: Whales are mammals, not fish.
The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs.
A tomato is a fruit to a botanist and a vegetable to a cook.

perspectives.who: Sorting by looks, as people did long ago
perspectives.explanation: Group living things by what they look like and where they live. This is easy to use. But it puts whales with fish.

perspectives.who: Sorting by family tree, as most biologists do today
perspectives.explanation: Group living things by who their relatives are. DNA is used to help check. This puts whales with hippos and mammals.
Some say a species is a group that can have babies together. Others say it is a branch of the family tree. Over twenty ideas exist, and no one rule works for bacteria, plants and animals.

explanations.art: A platypus in a river with arrows pointing to three boxes labelled mammal, bird and reptile, and a question mark.
explanations.context: Biologists sort plants and animals. This card shows that even experts disagree about where some living things belong.

explanations.definition: A quasicrystal is a solid with an ordered pattern that never repeats. It showed that the old two groups, crystal and glass, were not enough.
explanations.description: Sometimes a new thing does not fit any box. What should scientists do? In the 1980s, solids were sorted into two kinds. Crystals have atoms in a neat pattern that repeats, like tiles on a floor. Glass has atoms jumbled with no pattern. On 8 April 1982, an Israeli scientist, Dan Shechtman, looked at a metal with an electron microscope. He saw a pattern with five-fold symmetry, like a five-pointed star. A repeating tile pattern can never have this, so it should have been impossible. He wrote 'ten-fold???' in his notebook. Many scientists would not believe him, and he was asked to leave his research group. The famous chemist Linus Pauling said there were no quasicrystals, only quasi-scientists. But other laboratories made the same metal and saw the same pattern. In 1992, the International Union of Crystallography changed its definition of a crystal to make room. Shechtman won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2011. Later, natural quasicrystals were found in a meteorite from the far east of Russia. When a thing does not fit the boxes, the boxes can change.
examples: Crystal: a repeating pattern, like floor tiles.
Glass: no pattern at all.
Quasicrystal: an ordered pattern that never repeats, like some Penrose tilings.
explanations.art: A tiled floor with a regular repeating pattern next to a jumbled heap of tiles, and between them a pattern of star-shaped tiles that never repeats, with a scientist looking puzzled.
explanations.context: This card is about a scientist who found a material that fitted no group, and what happened next.

explanations.concept: Your body is a sorting machine
explanations.definition: Our bodies sort things by size and by pitch, using the shape of the parts inside. The brain makes groups too.
explanations.description: Your body sorts things all day, without being told. Your kidneys are like two small sieves. Blood flows through them. Small particles, like water and salts, pass through to become urine. The blood cells and big proteins stay in the blood. Your ear sorts too. Inside it is a coiled tube shaped like a snail. High sounds shake the start of the tube. Low sounds shake the far end. So your ear sorts sounds by pitch, before your brain even hears them. Your brain sorts all the time as well. Even babies a few months old start to treat dogs as one kind of thing and cats as another. How the brain makes its groups so quickly, from so little, is still not fully understood.
examples: Kidneys: sort blood by the size of the pieces.
The snail-shaped inner ear: sorts sounds from high to low.
The brain: sorts faces, voices and smells into groups.
explanations.art: A body outline with a kidney sieve, a coiled ear tube with high and low sounds marked along it, and a brain with little boxes.
explanations.context: Sorting is not only something we do with our hands. This card shows three ways your own body does it.

explanations.description: A sort is only as good as its rule, and someone chooses the rule. Many thinkers ask if the groups are out there in nature, waiting to be found, or if we make them up. The Greek thinker Plato wrote that a good thinker should divide things 'at the joints', like a good butcher. This means that nature has natural places to cut. Some groups, like the elements, really do seem natural. Every atom of gold has 79 protons. Other groups, such as 'vegetable', seem to depend on our needs. Putting a rock in a pile does not change the rock. Sorting people is different. When we put people into boxes using one rule, we can forget everything else about them. Computers sort too, and they learn their rules from the examples we give them. In 2018, Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested programs that sort faces. One program got about 35 in every 100 wrong for darker-skinned women. It got fewer than 1 in 100 wrong for lighter-skinned men. A likely reason is that the programs had learned from too few faces like theirs. A careful sorter asks: whose needs does this rule serve, and who does it leave out?
examples: A tomato is a fruit for a botanist and a vegetable for a cook.
A face program that works well for some people and badly for others.

perspectives.who: Plato, in ancient Greece, and many scientists
perspectives.explanation: Nature has joints, and a good sort cuts at them. Gold, hydrogen and the planets are real natural groups, found and not invented.

perspectives.who: Philosophers who think groups depend on our purposes
perspectives.explanation: Even good groups are partly made by us, because we choose what to notice. A botanist and a cook can both be right, because they sort for different jobs.

perspectives.who: People who study fairness in computers
perspectives.explanation: Whoever builds a sorting machine, or a form, builds their own view of the world into it. We should test it on everyone before we trust it.

explanations.art: A pair of hands holding a ring of string around some objects, and a second pair of hands drawing a different ring around the same objects.
explanations.context: Every sort needs someone to choose the rule. Are groups found in nature, or made by us? This card also asks what happens when the sorter is unfair.

explanations.concept: Other ways to sort the world
explanations.description: People in different places have sorted the world in different ways. More than two thousand years ago, Indian grammar writers such as Panini sorted the sounds of speech. They sorted them by where in the mouth each sound is made. The consonant rows of the Devanagari alphabet follow this. First come sounds made in the throat, like ka. Next come sounds made with the tongue on the palate, like cha. Then come sounds made with the tongue curled back, like the hard ta. Then come sounds made at the teeth, like the soft ta, and last, sounds made at the lips, like pa. Say ka, cha and pa slowly, and feel where each sound is made. Old Indian thinkers also sorted nature into five elements: earth, water, fire, air and space. The Greeks used four, without space. Chinese thinkers used five phases: wood, fire, earth, metal and water. Some people see a likeness with solid, liquid, gas and plasma. Earth is like solid. Water is like liquid. Air is like gas. Fire is like plasma. This is a likeness, not the same idea. The Greek elements were about qualities such as hot, cold, wet and dry. Today's sort of matter is about atoms. Each way of sorting tells us what its makers cared about.
examples: The Devanagari alphabet is sorted by where each sound is made.
The Greek four elements and the Indian five elements.

perspectives.explanation: Sounds are best grouped by how the mouth makes them. This sort is still used to teach the alphabet today.
The old elements of earth, water, fire and air are not what we now call elements. Today, elements are kinds of atom. But the old ideas helped people to ask questions.

explanations.art: A row of five lamps for earth, water, fire, air and space, beside the first row of the Devanagari alphabet with a mouth diagram showing the throat.
explanations.context: People have sorted the world in many different ways. This card gives a few, from India, Greece and China.

agreed.text: The same set of things can be sorted in many different ways, and the groups depend on the rule.
agreed.evidence: Try it with any heap at home. A brick is hard and dull. A glass bangle is hard and shiny. The groups change when the rule changes, and anyone can check it.

agreed.text: A rule is good when it gives the same answer for everyone who uses it.
agreed.evidence: Scientists write down exact tests, such as 'Does it scratch glass?'. Two people anywhere in the world get the same answer. That is how sorting can be repeated and trusted.

agreed.text: A good sort shows a pattern, and a pattern can help us predict things we have not found yet.
agreed.evidence: Mendeleev left gaps in his table in 1869. Gallium was found in 1875, scandium in 1879 and germanium in 1886. They matched what he had predicted.

agreed.text: There are 118 known kinds of atom, called elements. Everything we touch is made from them, and they can be sorted into the periodic table.
agreed.evidence: Chemists have found or made every one. The table's columns match how the atoms' outer electrons are arranged.

agreed.text: The colour of a star tells how hot its surface is.
agreed.evidence: In 1925, Cecilia Payne showed that the star types O, B, A, F, G, K and M are a row of temperatures. Astronomers have checked it with many telescopes since.

agreed.text: Sorting materials before recycling makes recycling work better.
agreed.evidence: Recycling plants sort first because each material is melted, shredded or pulped in its own way. Bits of glass mixed in with paper can spoil a whole batch of recycled paper.

challenging.claim: There is only one right way to sort any set of things.
challenging.who: A common way of thinking, and many school tests
challenging.for: A sort feels more tidy and clear when there is one right answer. Libraries need one shelf for each book.
challenging.against: A tomato is a fruit to a botanist and a vegetable to a cook. A brick is hard and dull at once. The right rule depends on the job.
challenging.context: Many people think there is one correct way to sort. This card looks at that idea.

challenging.who: Most people for thousands of years, and some old books
challenging.for: A whale lives in water, has fins and swims like a fish. Sorting by looks makes a whale a fish.
challenging.against: A whale breathes air, is warm-blooded and feeds its baby on milk. Linnaeus put whales with mammals in 1758. DNA shows the whale's closest living relative is the hippopotamus.
challenging.context: This card is about an old way of sorting whales, and why scientists gave it up.

challenging.claim: Pluto should still be called a planet.
challenging.who: Some astronomers, including Alan Stern, a leader of the mission that flew past Pluto in 2015
challenging.for: Pluto was called a planet for 76 years. It is round, it has moons, and it has mountains and an atmosphere. Many people feel the new rule was drawn to cut it out.
challenging.against: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union voted on a rule. A planet must orbit the Sun, be round, and have cleared other objects out of its path. Pluto shares its path with many other icy bodies, so it is now called a dwarf planet.
challenging.context: In 2006, astronomers changed the rule for sorting planets, and Pluto was moved to a new group. Some astronomers still disagree.

challenging.claim: Solids must have atoms in a pattern that repeats. A pattern that never repeats is impossible.
challenging.who: Most crystal scientists before 1982, and Linus Pauling, a famous chemist who won two Nobel Prizes
challenging.for: Every known crystal had a repeating pattern. Mathematicians had proved that a repeating pattern cannot have five-fold symmetry.
challenging.against: Dan Shechtman saw five-fold symmetry in a metal in 1982. Others repeated the test. Quasicrystals were even found in a meteorite. The official definition of a crystal was changed in 1992.
challenging.context: This card is about a scientist who was told his discovery was impossible. It did not fit the old groups.

challenging.claim: Dmitri Mendeleev alone invented the periodic table.
challenging.for: Mendeleev's 1869 table was the first to leave gaps and use them to predict new elements. These predictions came true.
challenging.against: Others had sorted elements before him. John Newlands, in England, spotted a repeating pattern in 1865 and was laughed at. Lothar Meyer in Germany made a very similar table at almost the same time. Mendeleev gets the credit because of his bold predictions.
challenging.context: Mendeleev is famous for the periodic table. This card asks who else helped, and why he gets the credit.

challenging.claim: The groups we use to sort the world are found in nature. We do not make them up.
challenging.for: Gold is gold wherever you find it. Every atom of hydrogen is the same. These look like real groups that nature made.
challenging.against: A group like 'vegetable' depends on what people want. Even 'species' has more than twenty definitions. Perhaps nature has natural groups only in some places.
challenging.context: Are the groups in nature, or do we make them? Thinkers have argued about this for over two thousand years.

challenging.claim: Glass is a very slow liquid. That is why old windows are thicker at the bottom.
challenging.who: Many people, and some old school books
challenging.for: Glass has no neat pattern of atoms, like a liquid. Some old windows are thicker at the bottom.
challenging.against: In 1998, Edgar Zanotto worked out that window glass would take longer than the age of the universe to sag. Old glass was made by hand, so it came out uneven. Builders often put the thick edge at the bottom. Some old windows are thicker at the top.
challenging.context: Glass is one of the tricky middle cases between solid and liquid. This card looks at a famous myth about it.

big_questions.q: A steel spoon and a wooden spoon look nothing alike. If you could zoom in until you saw only atoms, what would you find?
big_questions.hint: Both are made of atoms. Which kinds of atoms might each one have? How could anyone sort a spoon into kinds of atoms?

big_questions.q: Twenty good yes or no questions can find one thing out of more than a million. How can so few questions do so much?
big_questions.hint: Each good question cuts the number of possibilities in half. Try doubling a number twenty times.

big_questions.q: Astronomers sort stars by their light, and the types match the stars' colours. What are they really sorting?
big_questions.hint: A hot piece of iron glows red, then yellow, then white. What might colour tell you about a star?

big_questions.q: Elements in the same column of the periodic table behave alike. What might be the same inside them?
big_questions.hint: It is something about the outside of the atom, the part that touches other atoms.

big_questions.q: Is solid, liquid or gas something a material is, or something it is doing right now?
big_questions.hint: Think of water as ice, as water and as steam. It is the same stuff each time.

big_questions.q: Your ear sorts sounds before your brain does. How might a body part sort without a brain?
big_questions.hint: A sieve sorts by size: small things fall through its holes. What could a coiled tube do with sound?

big_questions.q: If a thing does not fit any group, should we change the thing or change the groups?
big_questions.hint: Remember quasicrystals and the platypus. What happened to the groups?

big_questions.q: Are the groups in nature waiting for us to find them, or do we make them up?
big_questions.hint: Is 'gold' a group nature made? What about 'vegetable'?

big_questions.q: Putting a rock in a pile does not change the rock. Can putting a person in a group change how others treat them?
big_questions.hint: A pile does not change a rock. What might a person feel? What does one rule hide about them?

big_questions.q: You belong to many groups at once, like a thing in many circles of a Venn diagram. Can any one group say everything about you?
big_questions.hint: Think of your family, your school, your favourite game and the language you speak. What does each group leave out?

big_questions.q: A kabadiwala makes money from things we call rubbish. Is there really such a thing as rubbish, or only things that have not been sorted yet?
big_questions.hint: What happens to a heap of mixed rubbish? What happens when it is sorted into piles?

big_questions.q: Mendeleev's gaps told chemists what to look for before anyone had seen it. Can a good pattern let you know something before you find it?
big_questions.hint: Think of a times table with one number missing, or a story with a missing page.

big_questions.q: In the story The Bell That Would Not Sing, Hira could hear high notes that her grandfather could not. Who in your family notices what others miss?
big_questions.hint: Every person sorts the world a little differently, because every person notices different things.

big_questions.q: When you sort a heap, who is doing the sorting? Can you find the part of you that notices?
big_questions.hint: Close your eyes and feel a spoon. Something notices the cold and the smooth. Where is the noticing?

roots.context: We have been learning to sort things into groups. Now we ask what sorting tells us about ourselves and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: Ask 'Is it hard?', and a steel spoon and a wooden spoon go in one group. Ask 'Is it shiny?', and they split apart. Neither spoon changed between the two sorts. So sharing a group shows only that two things gave the same answer to one question.
deep_truth.habit: We treat things in one group as the same kind of thing, as if the group told us what they are. A group only tells us how the things answered the one question we asked.
deep_truth.evidence: In One Heap, Three Rules, the same twelve things made different groups for each rule. The steel spoon and the wooden spoon were together under 'hard' and apart under 'shiny'.

three.who_am_i: You are a sorter. Your eyes, ears and hands sort the world all day, without being asked. You also belong to many groups at once, and no single group is all of you.
three.what_is_life: Living things are sorters. Your kidneys sort your blood and your ear sorts sounds. A living body keeps what it needs and lets the rest go.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is made of about a hundred kinds of atom, joined in endless ways. Sorting is how we find the order inside all that variety.

roots.thread: DeepKids believes that behind the many things in the world there is one source. Sorting points the same way. A heap of spoons, bangles and socks is many different things. Sort them by what they are made of, and they fall into a few materials. Sort the materials, and they come down to about a hundred kinds of atom. All of those atoms are built from just three kinds of tiny part: protons, neutrons and electrons.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka teaches his son Shvetaketu. By knowing one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. A pot and a plate differ only in name and shape. In the same way, by knowing one piece of a metal, you know all the ornaments made of it. By knowing one piece of iron, you know all things made of iron.
teachings.link: This is sorting by material. A pot and a plate look different, but they are one group when we ask 'What is it made of?'. The shape is one rule. The material is another.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4 (the Tittha Sutta) in the Pali Canon
teachings.teaching: Blind men each touch a different part of an elephant and each describes a different animal. Each is right about the part he touched and wrong about the whole.
teachings.link: Each sorting rule touches one part of a thing. Hard or soft, shiny or dull and metal or not all tell something true. No single rule tells the whole.

teachings.teaching: The way that can be spoken is not the eternal way. The name that can be named is not the eternal name.
teachings.link: Groups are names we give. They are useful, but the world does not have to fit them. The platypus did not fit the old groups, so biologists made a new group for it.

science.text: Almost every atom in your body, apart from hydrogen, was made inside a star. Margaret Burbidge, with Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle, showed how in 1957. So the many things in a heap are made from a few kinds of atom, and most of those were made in stars.
Whether the groups we use are found in nature or made by us is still argued by scientists and philosophers. Gold seems like a natural group. 'Vegetable' seems to depend on us.

other_view.who: Madhva, a philosopher of the Dvaita school in India, about 700 years ago
other_view.view: The differences between things are real and lasting. A pot is not clay in disguise. Madhva taught five real differences, such as between one soul and another and between matter and soul. In this view, sorting finds real differences. It does not only find different names for one thing.

practice.title: Sorting with eyes closed
practice.say: Close your eyes. I will put a thing in your hand. 1. Feel how cold or warm it is. 2. Feel if it is hard or soft, rough or smooth. 3. Feel how heavy it is. 4. Now I will tap it, so listen. 5. Say how you would sort this thing. 6. Open your eyes. You noticed all these differences. Who is the one who notices?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. A grown-up gives you a thing. Feel how cold it is. Feel if it is hard or soft. Listen to it tap. How would you sort it? Open your eyes. Who is the one who noticed?

ask: When you sort a heap, who is doing the sorting?
If you zoom in far enough, do the groups still exist?
Is the one who notices also in a group? Which one?
roots.art: A child sitting with eyes closed holding a spoon, with a faint glow around the hands, and behind the child a soft picture of stars becoming atoms becoming spoons.

story.title: The Bell That Would Not Sing
story.note: Tambapur, Kharsoli, Nana, Hira and this bell are imagined. The metals are real. Bell metal (kansa) is copper mixed with tin. Brass is copper mixed with zinc. They can look alike, but a kansa bowl rings for much longer than a brass one. Many people lose the ability to hear high sounds as they grow old.
text: Before I was a bell, I was a heap. I was forty-one lamps, a water tap, six door handles and a cart bell with a crack in it. I was also a great many bangles. I lay in the yard of a foundry in Tambapur, a town where every lane smells of hot metal. I did not know that I was going to be anything at all.

Every morning an old man came out to look at me. Everyone called him Nana, because every grandfather has to be called something. His eyes were sharp and his hands were sure. He meant to turn me into a school bell for the village of Kharsoli. The children there walked five kilometres to their lessons, and sometimes they arrived after the lessons had begun. 'A bell on the hill,' he said, 'and they will hear it from the far fields.'

A bell is made of bell metal, which is copper mixed with tin. But I was not all copper and tin. Some of my pieces were brass, which is copper mixed with zinc. Brass and bell metal look almost the same, the way two brothers do. So Nana sorted me. He did it the way he had done it for fifty years, with his eyes. Pale yellow pieces here. Red-gold pieces there. 'Colour does not lie,' he said. He tipped the red-gold pile into the furnace.

I remember the heat. Then the pour, a river of orange light running into a mould of clay. Then three days of waiting in the dark. Then the mould was broken. I stood in the sun for the first time, with the whole foundry looking at me.

Nana lifted a wooden mallet and struck me. I did not sing. I gave a short, flat 'clank', like a pot hit with a spoon, and then I was silent. He struck me again. 'Clank.' Somebody coughed. Nana put down the mallet and walked into the back room and shut the door.

The only one who stayed was his granddaughter, Hira. She was ten. She was not allowed near the furnace, so she had watched everything from the doorway. Now she walked all the way round me, the way you walk round a stranger. She knocked on me with her knuckle, and she listened. Then she went to the kitchen and came back with two bowls from her grandmother's shelf. One was a heavy yellow kansa bowl, the kind used for serving on feast days. The other was a brass bowl that looked exactly the same.

She hung each bowl from a loop of thread and tapped it with a pencil. The kansa bowl rang. It was a long, bright ringing, and it went on after the pencil had gone. The brass bowl rang too, but only for a moment, and then it stopped. 'Nana!' she called through the door. 'They look the same. But they are not the same.'

He opened the door a hand's width. 'Colour is what I can see,' he said slowly. 'The high sounds I cannot hear any more. That is why I trust my eyes.' Hira had never heard him say such a thing. 'But nobody will look at a bell from the far fields,' he went on, half to himself. 'They will only hear it.'
Hira took a breath. 'I can hear them,' she said. 'You tell me where to put each piece.'

So they sorted me again, all that was left of me, piece by piece. Hira hung each one from a string on the beam, tapped it with her pencil, shut her eyes and listened. 'Sings,' she said, and Nana laid the piece on a white cloth. 'Stops,' she said, and he laid the piece on a black one. Lamps. Handles. The tap. The bangles. By evening there were two piles. And they were not the piles that colour had made. Some red-gold pieces lay on the black cloth. Some pale ones lay on the white. Colour had been telling Nana something true. It just had not been telling him what a bell needs to know.

The short-ringing pile went off to be made into hinges and pots. The singing pile went into the fire. This time Nana let Hira stand at the door of the furnace room, with his hand on her shoulder. She watched the orange river pour. Three days. The mould was broken. Nana lifted the mallet, and then he did something I had not expected. He held it out to her.

She struck me once. I rang. It was not a clank. It was a note so clear and so long that it climbed the foundry roof and made the tin hum. It rolled out over the lane, where a dog lifted its head and the vegetable seller stopped weighing. It went on and on, thinning out like a thread drawn from a spool. When at last it ended, the lane was quiet for a moment, as if it were listening for more.

I hang now on a hill above Kharsoli, in a frame of iron. Each morning a child pulls my rope, and my voice goes out across the fields. Children come running from three villages. On my rim, in raised letters, is the name of the foundry. Nobody wrote Hira's name there. But stand underneath me and look up into the dark inside my rim. There you can find one small scratched letter. It was cut with a chisel by an old man who could no longer hear high notes. It is an H.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the pieces of metal never changed. Only the rule for sorting them changed. Sorted by colour, the heap hid the difference that mattered. Sorted by sound, the heap split into two piles, and the bell sang. A rule is only good when it fits the job. The story also asks who notices what. The old man trusted his eyes because his ears had changed. The girl's ears, and her willingness to speak, made the difference.
ask: Nana sorted the metal by colour. Why did it not work for a bell?
Hira sorted the metal by sound. Why did that rule fit the job better?
Some red-gold pieces went into the pile that stopped quickly. What does that tell you about sorting by colour?
Nana trusted his eyes because he could not hear high notes. What do you trust most, your eyes, your ears or your hands? When is each best?
Nana scratched a tiny H inside the bell. Why do you think he did it that way?

games.title: Rule Detective
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against a grown-up

printables.title: 24 thing cards to cut out, each with a picture and a name
12 secret rule cards
items: Is it hard? (a fingernail cannot mark it)
Is it made from a plant?
Does it make a ringing sound when tapped?
Is it smaller than your palm?

rules: Cut out the 24 thing cards and the 12 rule cards. Put the rule cards in a pile, face down.
One player is the Sorter. The Sorter secretly takes a rule card and does not show it.
The Sorter turns over thing cards one at a time. Each goes on the YES mat or the NO mat, by the secret rule. The Sorter says nothing about the rule.

After each card, the other players may guess the rule. A right guess after 3 cards wins 3 tokens. After 4 or 5 cards it wins 2 tokens. After 6 or more cards it wins 1 token. A wrong guess costs 1 token.

Any player may say 'Test it!'. Then the Sorter must show how they decided about that card. If you have the real thing at home, test it together. If the card was put in the wrong place, the Sorter loses a token.
When the rule is guessed, or after 8 cards, swap roles. Everyone should be the Sorter twice. The player with the most tokens wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the thing cards and the rule cards. 2. Lay the YES and NO mats side by side. 3. Put the rule cards face down in a pile. 4. Choose who is the Sorter first.
flow.say: Today we are detectives. One of us secretly picks a rule. The rest must work out the rule, just by watching where things go.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Put the YES and NO mats down. One player is the Sorter. The others are detectives.
flow.context: This is the first step of Rule Detective. It is a card game about sorting. One player sorts things by a secret rule, and the others guess the rule.

flow.do: Play a practice round with everyone watching. Put the steel spoon, glass bangle, foil ball and brass lota on the YES mat. Put the wooden spoon, rubber band and woollen sock on the NO mat. Ask what the rule is.
flow.say: Look at the YES mat and the NO mat. Can you work out the secret rule?
flow.kid: Look at what is on the YES mat. Look at what is on the NO mat. What is the secret rule? Tap your answer.

ask.q: How did you work out the rule?
good: I looked for what the YES things all have that the NO things do not.
I tried a rule in my head and checked it on every card.

check.q: YES: steel spoon, glass bangle, foil ball, brass lota. NO: wooden spoon, rubber band, woollen sock. What is the rule?
check.why: Every YES thing is shiny, and every NO thing is dull. The rule is 'Is it shiny?'. 'Is it hard?' fails, because the foil ball is soft and the wooden spoon is hard. 'Is it made of metal?' fails, because the glass bangle is not metal. Picking either one usually means the detective did not check the rule on every card.

flow.do: 1. The Sorter takes a rule card in secret and starts turning over thing cards, one at a time. 2. After each card, the detectives may guess. 3. Count tokens as in the rules. 4. When a rule is guessed, swap roles.
flow.say: Sorter, put each card where it belongs by your secret rule. Detectives, think about each card before you guess.
flow.kid: Sorter, pick a secret rule. Put cards on YES or NO. Detectives, watch carefully. Guess the rule when you are ready.
flow.parent: Let the Sorter be a child, so they think hard about their own rule. If the Sorter is unsure about a card, say 'Test it!' and do the test together. Rules with an exact test, like the fingernail test, are the fairest.

flow.do: Pause on a card that was hard to place, such as the candle, the plastic bottle or the coconut shell. Ask how the Sorter decided.
flow.say: That one was a tricky middle. How did the Sorter decide where it went? What could we do with a card like that?
flow.kid: Some cards are tricky. Which card was hardest to place? How did you decide?

ask.q: What can we do with a card that sits between YES and NO?
good: Use a test.
Make a middle pile.
Make the rule more exact.

flow.think: Could two different rules put all the cards in the same places? What card would show them apart?

flow.do: Count the tokens to find the winner. Then look at the rule cards you used.
flow.say: Which rules were easy to guess? Which were hard? Was a rule with a test fairer than a rule without one?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who won? Which rule was hardest to guess?
flow.think: Why is 'Is it pretty?' a bad rule for this game?

games.context: This is a card game about sorting. One player secretly picks a rule and sorts things by it. The other players watch and try to work out the rule.

setup.art: A table with 24 picture cards in a pile, two paper mats marked YES and NO, and a pile of face-down rule cards.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the YES and NO mats. Put the cards beside them.

setup.art: A child turning over a picture card of a steel spoon and putting it on the YES mat, while two friends watch closely.
setup.caption: 2. The Sorter puts each card on YES or NO by a secret rule.

setup.art: A friend holding up a hand to say 'Test it!' while the Sorter presses a fingernail into a candle.
setup.caption: 3. Guess the rule. Say 'Test it!' if a card looks wrong.

games.title: Find the Missing Card
games.players: 1 to 4 players, one of them the Keeper

printables.title: 12 Zib cards to cut out. Zibs are made-up materials from a made-up planet.
A table with 3 rows and 4 columns

rules: Cut out the 12 Zib cards. The Keeper secretly takes away Zib 6, Zib 7 and Zib 12. The Keeper hides them face down and does not say which ones.
The other players put the 9 cards that are left in number order, in rows of four. They leave a gap wherever a number is missing.
Look down each column. What is the same? What changes as you go down?
For each gap, write a guess on the guess sheet. Guess the border colour and the bounce number of the missing Zib.
The Keeper turns over the hidden cards. Score 1 point for each correct colour and 1 point for each correct bounce number. The player with the most points wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 Zib cards. 2. The Keeper hides Zib 6, Zib 7 and Zib 12 face down, without showing the others. 3. Put the table sheet on the floor.
flow.say: These are Zibs, materials from a made-up planet. A real scientist once did this with the elements of our world. Today we are going to find the missing cards by thinking.
flow.kid: Cut out the Zib cards. The Keeper hides three of them. Lay the table sheet out. Now the detective work begins.
flow.context: This is the first step of Find the Missing Card. This game copies what Mendeleev did when he sorted the elements. Zibs are made-up materials, so you can practise the idea.

flow.do: 1. Put the 9 cards on the table, in order of their numbers, four to a row. 2. Leave a gap where a number is missing. 3. Look down each column.
flow.say: Put the cards in number order, four in each row. Now look down the first column. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Put the cards in number order, four in a row. Leave a gap where a card is missing. Look down each column. What do you see?

ask.q: What do you notice about the cards in each column?
good: They have the same coloured border.
The bounce number goes up by 2 as you go down.

check.q: Zib 1, Zib 5 and Zib 9 sit in the same column. What is the same about them?
options: They all have a red border
They all have the same bounce number
They all have the same number
check.why: Zib 1, 5 and 9 all have a red border. Their bounce numbers are 2, 4 and 6, so they are not the same. Picking 'same bounce number' usually means the detective noticed the pattern but not what stays the same and what changes. The border colour stays the same. The bounce number goes up by 2.

flow.do: 1. Look at each gap. 2. For each gap, work out the border colour from the column. 3. Work out the bounce number from the numbers above and below. 4. Write the guesses on the guess sheet.
flow.say: Mendeleev did this with real elements. A gap is not a problem. A gap is a clue. What colour should the missing card have? What bounce should it have?
flow.kid: Look at each gap. Which colour belongs in its column? What bounce number fits the pattern? Write your guesses.
flow.parent: The colour of a gap comes from its column. The bounce number goes up by 2 at each step down a column. Zib 6 is in the blue column. Zib 2 above it has bounce 3, so Zib 6 should have bounce 5. Zib 7 is in the green column, between bounce 1 and bounce 5, so it should have bounce 3. Zib 12 is in the yellow column, below bounce 5 and bounce 7, so it should have bounce 9.

flow.do: The Keeper turns over the hidden cards. Compare them with the guesses and count the points.
flow.say: Turn over the hidden cards. Did the pattern tell us what was missing before we saw it?
flow.kid: Turn over the hidden cards. Were you right? Count your points.
flow.think: Mendeleev's gaps came true when gallium, scandium and germanium were found. What if a card turned out to be different from the pattern? What should the sorter do?

flow.do: Talk about what a good pattern lets you do.
flow.say: A good sort does more than tidy things up. It lets you guess what you have not found. Where else could a pattern tell you what is missing?
flow.kid: A good sort lets you guess what you have not found yet. Where else could a pattern help you?
flow.think: Think of a times table with one number missing, or a row of beads with one bead gone.

games.context: This is a card game that copies what Mendeleev did in 1869. He sorted the elements into a table with gaps, and used the pattern to predict elements nobody had found yet.

items.p: What is a sorting rule?
opts: A question that every thing can answer, to decide its group
A rule about how to tidy up
items.why: A sorting rule is a question, such as 'Is it shiny?'. Each thing is checked against it and goes in a group. Picking 'the name of the group' usually means the group and the rule have been mixed up. The group is the result. The rule is the question that makes it.

items.p: A brick is in the hard group when we sort by hard or soft. It is in the dull group when we sort by shiny or dull. Why?
opts: The rule changed, and the brick stayed the same
One of the sorts is wrong
items.why: The brick did not change. Each rule asks a different question about it. Hard asks one question and dull asks another. Both groups are right. Picking 'one of the sorts is wrong' usually means the child expects only one right way to sort.

items.p: A good sorting rule has a clear yes or no ____.
items.why: A good rule gives a clear answer, yes or no, and the same answer whoever asks.

items.p: Is it made of metal? Sort these things.
items.why: Steel, iron and aluminium are metals. Wood, glass and plastic are not. The glass bangle is shiny like metal, but shiny is a different rule.

items.p: Is it shiny? Sort these things.
items.why: Shiny things show a bright reflection. Dull things do not. Notice that the glass bangle is shiny but not metal, and the foil ball is shiny and metal.

items.p: Which of these is a good rule for sorting?
items.why: 'Is it shiny?' has a clear answer that anyone can check by looking. The others depend on who is asked. A rule should give the same answer for everyone.

items.p: One thing can be in different groups under different rules.
items.why: True. A steel spoon is in the shiny group, the hard group and the metal group. The spoon stays the same. Each rule asks a different question.

items.p: If a thing does not fit any group, the best thing to do is throw it away.
items.why: False. A thing that does not fit is useful. It may mean the rule is not clear, or that a new group is needed. Scientists have made new groups because of tricky things.

items.p: Match each tricky thing to the best way to deal with it.
pairs: A candle is hard, but a fingernail can mark it
Use a test and let the test decide
A plastic cup is a little bendy
items.why: A test settles a tricky case fairly. A more exact rule says what counts. A middle group is for things that are truly between. All three are used by scientists.

items.p: In a Venn diagram of Shiny and Hard, where does a steel spoon go?
items.why: A steel spoon is shiny and hard. It fits both rules, so it goes in the overlap. Picking one circle only usually means the second rule was forgotten.

items.p: In a Venn diagram of Shiny and Hard, where does a woollen sock go?
items.why: A woollen sock is soft and dull. It fits neither rule, so it goes outside both circles. Picking the overlap is common. Some children think the overlap is the place for odd things, but it is for things that fit both.

items.p: Look at the Carroll table. How many things are dull and soft?
items.why: The box where Dull meets Soft holds five things: rubber band, woollen sock, cotton hanky, candle and paper cup. Picking 3 usually means the Dull and Hard box was read. Always check both labels.
items.context: In the experiment One Heap, Three Rules, you sort twelve things by hard or soft and then by shiny or dull. A Carroll table has four boxes, one for each pair of answers.

items.p: In a branching key, each question splits the group in ____.
items.why: A good question splits the group into two smaller groups, ideally of equal size.

items.p: A key starts: 'Is it hard?' If yes: 'Is it shiny?' Yes is ice, no is a brick. If the first answer is no: 'Is it waterproof?' Yes is a balloon, no is paper. What is a hard, shiny thing?
items.why: Follow the key. Hard, so yes. Shiny, so yes. That leads to ice. A brick is hard but not shiny. The balloon and the paper are not hard.
items.context: A branching key is a chart of yes or no questions. You follow the answers, one step at a time, until you reach one thing.

items.p: Put the steps of making a branching key in order.
items: Ask a question that splits them in half
Add a question to each branch
Test the key with a friend
items.why: First choose the things. Then ask a question that splits them in half. Keep adding questions on each branch until each thing is alone. Last, test the key on someone else.

items.p: A kabadiwala keeps paper, glass and iron in different piles. Why?
opts: Each is sold to a different buyer and recycled in its own way
items.why: Each material is recycled in its own way, so each pile goes to a different buyer. Picking 'he likes tidy piles' is partly true, but the real reason is the job the sort is for.

items.p: A farmer tosses grain in a flat basket and the husk blows away. What rule is the wind using?
opts: Light things blow away more than heavy things
items.why: Wind moves light things much more than heavy things. So the husk blows away and the grain falls back. Picking 'big things' is common, but a big thing can be light or heavy. Weight is what matters here.

items.p: Pick five things from your pencil box or bag. Sort them in two different ways. Write the rule you used each time.
items.a: Any two clear rules with sorted lists. For example: Rule 1, made of plastic or not. Rule 2, longer than my hand or not.
items.why: Any two rules with yes or no answers, and groups that match the rules, are right.

items.p: Draw a Venn diagram with two circles, 'Round' and 'Red'. Put four things in it.
items.a: Two overlapping circles. A tomato or a red ball in the overlap. A red book in Red only. A coin in Round only. A pencil outside.
items.why: A Venn diagram needs overlapping circles, labels and things placed by both rules.

items.p: Look at the Carroll table from a child's experiment. Which box has the most things?
items.why: The Soft and dull box has five things. The others have three, three and one. Picking Hard and shiny usually means the first box was chosen without counting.
items.context: In the experiment One Heap, Three Rules, you sort twelve things by hard or soft and then by shiny or dull. A Carroll table has four boxes, one for each pair of answers.

items.p: In the Carroll table, 3 + 3 + 1 + 5 = ____ things were sorted altogether.
items.why: 3 plus 3 is 6. 6 plus 1 is 7. 7 plus 5 is 12. Every thing goes in exactly one box, so the boxes add up to the whole heap.
