items.p: In the Scratch Ladder, a fingernail marks soap but not a plastic comb. A steel nail marks the comb. Which is harder?
items.why: The comb was not marked by the fingernail, but the soap was. So the comb is harder. Picking the soap usually means the ladder was read upside down. A thing that is marked more easily is softer.
items.context: In the experiment The Scratch Ladder, you try to scratch eight things with a fingernail and then a steel nail. This puts them in order from softest to hardest.

items.p: Put these on the right rung of the Scratch Ladder.
cats: Rung 2: only a steel nail marks it
Rung 3: even a steel nail does not mark it
items: Rung 2: only a steel nail marks it
Rung 2: only a steel nail marks it
Rung 3: even a steel nail does not mark it
Rung 3: even a steel nail does not mark it
items.why: Soap and candle are marked by a fingernail. Wood and plastic need the steel nail. The glaze on a ceramic mug and a glass jar resist even that.
items.context: In the Scratch Ladder, three rungs show how hard a thing is. The first rung is softest and the third is hardest.

items.p: Key A asks 'Is it hard?' first and then splits each half again. Key B asks about one thing at a time. For eight things, which key never needs more than three questions?
items.why: Key A halves the group each time: 8, 4, 2, 1. So it needs at most three questions. Key B can need seven. Picking Key B usually means counting the lucky first guess and forgetting the unlucky ones.
items.context: In the Twenty Questions Race, Key A splits eight things in half each time. Key B picks out one thing at a time.

items.p: Each good question doubles the number of things a key can tell apart. With four questions, a key can tell apart ____ things.
items.why: One question tells 2 apart, two tell 4, three tell 8 and four tell 16. Doubling each time.
items.context: In the Twenty Questions Race, you count how many questions a key needs. Each good question cuts the number of possibilities in half.

items.p: Eight things. Four are hard: steel spoon, wooden spoon, plastic comb and glass bangle. Four are soft: rubber band, woollen sock, cotton hanky and candle. Which first question is best for a key?
items.why: 'Is it hard?' splits the eight things into four and four. The best first question cuts the group in half. The others pick out just one or two things.

items.p: Two bowls look the same. One rings for a long time when tapped. The other rings only for a moment. What does this show?
opts: Sorting by sound can show a difference that sorting by looks misses
The bowls must be the same material
items.why: Looks and sounds are different rules. They can sort the same things into different groups. Picking 'the bowls must be the same material' usually means trusting looks too much.
items.context: In the experiment Sort by Sound, you hang things on a thread and tap them lightly. You listen to how long they ring, and sort them by sound.

items.p: Cornflour and water flows slowly, but feels hard if you punch it. Which group does it belong in?
opts: A tricky middle group, soft matter
items.why: It acts like a liquid and like a solid, depending on how fast you move it. Scientists put things like this in a group called soft matter. Picking solid or liquid ignores what the other test showed.

items.p: Rice pours like water, so rice is a liquid.
items.why: False. Each grain is a hard solid. A pile of grains can flow because the grains slide over each other, but each one keeps its shape.

items.p: In 1869, Mendeleev left some empty places in his table of elements. Why?
opts: He thought undiscovered elements would fill them
items.why: He saw a pattern, and the pattern had gaps. He said new elements would be found to fit. Gallium, scandium and germanium were found later, and matched. Picking 'forgot' misses that the gaps were on purpose, and that they were a prediction.

items.p: Match each person to what they sorted.
pairs: the elements, into the periodic table
stars, by the pattern of their light
plants and animals, into groups inside groups
the sounds of speech, by where the mouth makes them
items.why: Mendeleev sorted atoms in 1869. Cannon sorted about 350,000 stars. Linnaeus sorted living things in the 1700s. Panini, an Indian grammarian, sorted the sounds of Sanskrit more than two thousand years ago.

items.p: Which star is hottest on its surface?
items.why: Blue-white stars are the hottest. Red stars are the coolest. Picking red is very common, because red makes us think of fire. But a piece of iron that glows red is the coolest a glowing thing can be. Heated more, it glows yellow, then white.
items.context: Astronomers can tell how hot a star's surface is from its colour. Blue-white means hot and red means cooler.

items.p: A whale lives in water and has fins. Why do scientists call it a mammal and not a fish?
opts: It breathes air and feeds its baby on milk
items.why: Scientists sort by who the whale is related to, not only by how it looks. A whale breathes air, is warm-blooded and nurses its young. Picking 'very big' or 'cold water' uses things that are not what scientists sort by.

items.p: A botanist says a tomato is a fruit. A cook says it is a vegetable. Can both be right? Explain.
items.a: Yes. They use different rules for different jobs. A botanist sorts by how the plant grows seeds. A cook sorts by taste and how food is used in meals.
items.why: A sort depends on the rule and the job. Both rules can be right for their own purposes.

items.p: Design three questions for a key. A blind person must be able to use it to tell apart a spoon, a cloth and a stone. Use touch or sound only.
items.a: For example: Is it cold when I touch it? Does it ring when I tap it? Is it soft when I squeeze it?
items.why: Good answers use touch or sound, and each question has a clear yes or no answer.

items.p: Which tool sorts these? Choose the best tool for each.
items: plastic caps that float from stones that sink
items.why: Each tool uses a different rule. A magnet picks out certain metals. A sieve sorts by size. Wind sorts by weight. Water sorts by whether a thing floats.

items.p: Put these stars in order, from hottest to coolest. Rigel is blue-white. The Sun is yellow. Betelgeuse is red. Sirius is white.
items.why: Blue-white Rigel is hottest. White Sirius is next. The yellow Sun is cooler. Red Betelgeuse is coolest of these four. The order follows the star types B, A, G, M.

items.p: Why must we use the same test on every thing when we sort?
opts: So the groups show how the things differ, and not how we tested
So we can change our mind
items.why: If every thing has a different test, a difference in the groups could come from the test and not from the things. The same test makes it fair. Picking 'change our mind' misses the point of a fair test.

items.p: In 2006 astronomers changed the rule for a planet, and Pluto was moved to a new group. What does this show?
opts: Groups depend on rules, and rules can be changed
items.why: Pluto did not change. The rule did. A rule is a human choice, and scientists can revise it when they learn more. Some astronomers still argue that the rule is wrong. Picking 'Pluto changed' is a common idea, but Pluto is the same as before.
items.context: Pluto was called a planet for 76 years. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union voted on a new rule, and Pluto became a dwarf planet.

items.p: Dan Shechtman found a solid with a pattern that never repeats. The old two groups were crystal and glass. What did scientists finally do?
opts: Changed the definition of a crystal to make room for it
Put it in the glass group
items.why: After other scientists checked his work, the official definition of a crystal was changed in 1992. The boxes were changed to fit the discovery. Picking 'put it in the glass group' ignores that the metal had a clear pattern.
items.context: Crystals have a repeating pattern, like floor tiles. Glass has no pattern. A quasicrystal has a pattern that never repeats.

items.p: Glass is a slow liquid, so old windows are thicker at the bottom.
items.why: False. Calculations show window glass would take longer than the age of the universe to sag. Old windows are uneven because of how they were made.
items.context: Glass is a tricky middle case between solid and liquid. A famous myth says it flows very slowly.

items.p: Sodium and potassium are in the same column of the periodic table. Why do they behave alike?
opts: They have the same number of outer electrons
They were found on the same day
items.why: Outer electrons decide how an atom joins with others. Atoms in the same column have the same pattern of outer electrons, so they act alike. Picking 'same weight' is an easy mistake, because the table was first sorted by weight. But weights are different in a column.
items.context: The periodic table sorts atoms into columns. Atoms in the same column behave alike.

items.p: How many elements did Mendeleev's gaps help scientists find, among those he predicted?
items.why: Between 1875 and 1886, gallium, scandium and germanium were found, and they matched his predictions closely. A pattern that predicts is much stronger than one that only tidies.

items.p: Annie Jump Cannon sorted stars into seven types by their light. What did Cecilia Payne show in 1925 about these types?
opts: They are really a row of temperatures
They are a row of sizes
They are a row of ages
They are a row of distances
items.why: Payne showed that the types are about how hot the surface of the star is. She also showed that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Picking 'sizes' or 'distances' is a common guess, but the types show heat.

items.p: Some computer programs that sort faces worked well for lighter-skinned men and badly for darker-skinned women. What was the likely cause?
opts: The program was taught with too few faces like theirs
Dark skin is harder to see in dark rooms only
items.why: A program learns its rules from the examples it is given. If most examples look one way, it works best for them. Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru showed this in 2018. It is a lesson in who is left out when the rule is built.
items.context: Computers sort pictures into groups by learning from many examples. In 2018, two researchers tested programs that sort faces.

items.p: A pile does not change a rock. But a label can change how people treat a person. Why should we be careful when we sort people?
items.a: A person has many parts to them, and one rule hides most of them. People can feel hurt or left out. A sort can also be used unfairly.
items.why: Good answers say that people belong to many groups at once, and that a single rule hides the rest. They may also mention fairness or feelings.

items.p: Nana sorted the metal by colour and Hira sorted it by sound. Why did the bell sing only after the second sort?
items.a: Colour showed what the metal looked like, but not what it would sound like. A bell needs bell metal, which rings. Hira's sort used the property the bell needed.
items.why: The rule must fit the job. A bell is for sound, so sorting by sound fits.

items.p: Ketchup stays in the bottle until you shake it. In what way is it a tricky middle case?
opts: It acts like a solid when still and a liquid when moved
items.why: Ketchup is part of the soft matter group. It holds its shape when still and flows when shaken. Picking 'a gas' mixes up thick with light and airy.

items.p: Your kidneys sort blood by size. Which stays in the blood?
items.why: Small particles like water and salts pass through the sieve-like kidney. The big blood cells stay in the blood. Picking 'everything leaves' misses that sorting keeps something and lets go of something else.

items.p: Twenty good yes or no questions can tell apart more than a million things. Why?
opts: Each good question halves the possibilities, and twenty halvings take more than a million things down to one
items.why: One question tells 2 apart, ten tell 1,024 apart, and twenty tell 1,048,576 apart. Doubling grows very fast. Picking 'each question adds a hundred' mixes up adding with doubling.

items.p: Design a sorting line for a pile of rubbish containing paper, steel tins, glass bottles and plastic bottles. Say the rule at each step.
items.a: Step 1: blow, or use a fan, to move the light paper. Step 2: a magnet attracts the steel tins. Step 3: a tub of water, where plastic bottles with their caps on float and glass sinks. Other sensible orders are right too.
items.why: Any sensible order with a clear rule at each step is right.

items.p: Draw a branching key for four fruits: mango, banana, guava, apple. Use yes or no questions.
items.a: For example, 'Do you peel it before eating?' Yes gives mango or banana, split by 'Is it long and curved?'. No gives guava or apple, split by 'Is it red outside?'.
items.why: A key splits the group at each question until each fruit is alone. The questions must have clear yes or no answers.

items.p: A star that looks red is hotter than a star that looks blue.
items.why: False. Red stars are cooler. Blue-white stars are hotter. In the same way, a piece of iron glows red first, and only glows white when it is much hotter.
items.context: Astronomers use star colour to tell how hot a star's surface is.

items.p: A girl can hear what her grandfather cannot, so she helps him sort the metal. What does this show about sorting?
opts: Different people notice different things, and each can help
items.why: Each person notices different things. Together they sorted better than either could alone. Picking 'hearing is better than seeing' mistakes one good rule for a rule that is always best.
items.context: In the story The Bell That Would Not Sing, Nana trusted his eyes because he could not hear high sounds. His granddaughter Hira could.

experiments.title: One Heap, Three Rules
experiments.question: If we sort the same twelve things in different ways, does each thing always land in the same group?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess two things, and say why you think so. Will the hard group be the same size as the shiny group? Will any thing land in the same kind of group every time?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same twelve things every time. Write the rule before you start sorting. Use the same test for every thing, in the same way. Change only the rule.

materials.item: twelve things, each made of only one material, for example a steel spoon, a wooden spoon, a plastic comb, a glass bangle, a rubber band, a woollen sock, a cotton hanky, a candle, a clay diya, a pebble (a small stone from a potted plant, or a wooden toy block), a foil ball and a paper cup
two sheets of paper, labelled for the groups
a pencil and the results table
a phone or camera to photograph each sort

experiments.safety: Choose things with no sharp edges. Keep glass things low, over a soft rug.

schedule.what: Guess. Sort the twelve things three ways. Fill in the table. Make a tally and a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Count the things in each group and make a tally. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each box of the Carroll table.

flow.do: 1. Collect twelve things, each made of just one material. 2. Put them in a heap on the floor. 3. Ask your child to guess the two things in the Predict step.
flow.say: Here is a heap of twelve things. We are going to sort them three times, with three different rules. What do you think will happen?
flow.kid: Make a heap of twelve things. Guess how big each group will be. Guess if any thing stays in the same kind of group.

ask.q: Do you think one thing could be in a different group every time?
good: Yes, a spoon can be hard and shiny and metal, all at once.
It depends on the rule.

flow.context: This is the first step of One Heap, Three Rules. You sort the same twelve things three ways, to see that the rule decides the group.

flow.do: 1. Write the rule 'Is it hard?' on a sheet. Explain the test: press a fingernail into each thing. If it leaves a mark, it is soft. 2. Test each thing. 3. Put the hard things on one sheet and the soft ones on the other. 4. Photograph the groups and write them in the results table.
flow.say: Here is a fair test for hard and soft. Press a fingernail into it. If it leaves a mark, it is soft. We will use the same test on every single thing.
flow.kid: Rule 1: hard or soft. Press your fingernail into each thing. A mark means soft. No mark means hard. Make two groups.
flow.parent: Some things are tricky. A candle takes a fingernail mark, so it is soft by this test, even though it feels solid. A foil ball may surprise you too: it is shiny, but it takes a fingernail mark. Let the test decide, not the guess.

check.q: Why do we use the same fingernail test on every thing?
check.why: If every thing had a different test, the groups would show how we tested, not how the things differ. The same test makes the sort fair. Picking another answer usually means the point of a fair test has not been seen yet.

flow.do: 1. Mix all twelve things again. 2. Write the rule 'Is it shiny?' on a sheet. Decide the test. Does it show a clear picture of your face, or a bright spot of light from a torch? 3. Sort. 4. Photograph the groups and record them.
flow.say: Mix them all up. This time the question is: is it shiny? If you can see your face in it, or a bright spot of light, it is shiny.
flow.kid: Rule 2: shiny or dull. Mix up all the things. Is it shiny? Can you see your face in it? Sort into two groups.
flow.parent: Notice that the groups are not the same as before. A steel spoon is hard and shiny. A foil ball is soft and shiny. A wooden spoon is hard and dull.

flow.do: 1. Mix the things again. 2. Ask your child to choose a rule of their own with an exact test. 3. Sort the things. 4. Write the rule and the groups in the results table.
flow.say: Now choose your own rule. It must have a yes or no answer, and a test everyone can use.
flow.kid: Rule 3: you choose. Make a rule with a yes or no answer. Think of a test for it. Sort all twelve things.

ask.q: What is your rule, and what is the test?
good: Does it sink in water?
Is it made of metal?
Does it bend when I press it?
Does it feel cold when I touch it?

flow.parent: Good rules include: Does it float? Is it smaller than my palm? Can I see through it? Does it make a noise when tapped? Rules like 'Is it nice?' do not work because they have no test.

flow.do: 1. Make a Carroll table with the results of Rule 1 and Rule 2, using four boxes. 2. Write each thing in the right box. 3. Count the things in each box and make tally marks. 4. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each box.
flow.say: Put each thing into one of four boxes: hard and shiny, hard and dull, soft and shiny, soft and dull. Then let's count the things in each box.
flow.kid: Make a table with four boxes. Put each thing in its box. Count the things in each box. Draw a bar for each box.

check.q: A thing is in the 'soft and shiny' box of the Carroll table. Which two rules does it fit?
check.why: The 'soft and shiny' box holds things that passed the soft test and the shiny test. Picking 'hard, and shiny' usually means one row was read wrongly. Always read both labels, the column and the row.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how many things in each box
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: You sorted the same twelve things three times. Tell me three things. What do you think decides which group a thing goes in? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the rule decides the group. What I saw: the foil ball was shiny but soft, and the wooden spoon was hard but dull. Why: hard and shiny are different questions, so one thing can be in different groups.
flow.think: Which thing was hardest to place? How did the test help?

experiments.context: In this experiment you sort the same twelve things three times, with three different rules. You find out that the rule, and not only the thing, decides which group it lands in.

experiments.title: The Scratch Ladder
experiments.question: Can a test settle where a tricky thing belongs? Can we put things in order from softest to hardest?
experiments.predict: Before you test, put your eight things in a line. Put the one you think is softest first and the hardest last. Say why you put each one there.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same tool on every thing, with the same push, over the same short scratch. Try each thing twice. Test the fingernail first, then the steel nail.
results_table: Does a steel nail scratch it?

materials.item: eight things: a bar of soap, a piece of chalk or a crayon, a candle, an aluminium foil food container, a wooden spoon, a plastic comb, a glazed ceramic mug and a glass jar
a steel nail, held only by a grown-up or with a grown-up watching
a phone camera to zoom in on marks, or a magnifying glass if you have one
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up holds the steel nail or watches closely. Scratch away from your body. Drag gently on the mug and the jar, and do not press hard on glass. Do not scratch things that are precious or that belong to someone else.

schedule.what: Guess the order. Test each thing with a fingernail, then a steel nail. Build the ladder.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a ladder with three rungs. Write the names of the things on the right rung.

flow.do: 1. Put the eight things on a tray. 2. Ask your child to line them up from softest to hardest, by guessing. 3. Take a photo of the line.
flow.say: These eight things are all different. Which do you think is softest? Which is hardest? Put them in a line.
flow.kid: Put the eight things in a line. Softest on the left. Hardest on the right. Take a photo.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Scratch Ladder. You use two scratch tests to put things in order from softest to hardest.

flow.do: 1. Press a fingernail firmly into each thing and drag it a short way. 2. Look closely for a mark, or zoom in with a phone camera. 3. Write yes or no in the table.
flow.say: First test: your fingernail. Press and drag it a little way. Look closely. Is there a mark?
flow.kid: Test one: your fingernail. Press and drag it over each thing. Look closely. Is there a mark? Write yes or no.
flow.parent: A scratch is a groove. Chalk and soap leave powder, but they are still marked. The mug may show a faint line from your fingernail. Wipe it with a finger. If it wipes off, it is not a scratch.

ask.q: Which things did your fingernail mark?
good: The soap, the chalk, the candle and the foil container.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up holds the steel nail. 2. Use the nail on only the things that the fingernail did not mark. 3. Press and drag the same way. 4. Look closely, or zoom in with a phone camera, and write yes or no.
flow.say: Second test: a steel nail. We use it only on the things that the fingernail could not mark. A grown-up holds the nail.
flow.kid: Test two: a steel nail. A grown-up holds it. Use it on the things your fingernail could not mark. Look for a scratch.

check.q: A thing is marked by the steel nail but not by a fingernail. Compared with a thing marked by a fingernail, it is…
check.why: The fingernail marks only the softest things. If the steel nail is needed, the thing is harder than those. Picking 'softer' usually means the ladder was read upside down. The higher the rung, the harder the thing.

flow.do: 1. Draw a ladder with three rungs. 2. Write the things on the right rung. Rung 1: a fingernail marks it. Rung 2: only the steel nail marks it. Rung 3: even the steel nail does not mark it. 3. Compare with the guessed line.
flow.say: Here is the scratch ladder. Rung one is softest, and rung three is hardest. Put each thing on its rung. Was your guessed line right?
flow.kid: Draw a ladder with three rungs. Rung 1 is softest. Rung 3 is hardest. Put each thing on its rung. Compare with your guess.
flow.parent: Expect soap, chalk, candle and the foil container on rung 1. Expect the wooden spoon and plastic comb on rung 2. Expect the mug and the glass jar on rung 3. The nail may leave a grey line of metal on the glass. It wipes off, so it is not a scratch. A different result is fine. Wood and plastics vary a lot.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: You tested eight things with a fingernail and a steel nail. Tell me three things. What do you think now about hard and soft? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a test puts things in a clear order. What I saw: the fingernail marked the soap and the candle, but not the mug. Why: a harder thing cannot be scratched by a softer thing. In 1812, a German scientist named Friedrich Mohs used this idea to make a ladder of ten minerals. It runs from soft talc to diamond. Diamond is at the top, because it scratches every other mineral.
flow.think: If a candle is at the bottom of our ladder, where would a diamond be?

experiments.context: In this experiment you put eight things in order from softest to hardest, using a fingernail and a steel nail. A test like this settles tricky cases, like the candle.

experiments.title: Twenty Questions Race: which key is fastest?
experiments.question: Which first question makes the fastest branching key?
experiments.predict: Before you play, guess, and say why you think so. Which key finds a secret object in fewer questions? One key splits eight things into four and four. The other picks out one thing at a time.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same eight things for both keys. Each thing is picked once for each key. The same person answers all the questions. Change only the key.

materials.item: eight things: a steel spoon, a wooden spoon, a plastic comb, a glass bangle, a rubber band, a woollen sock, a cotton hanky and a candle
two big sheets of paper and a marker, to draw the two keys
a second person to pick the secret thing
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Nothing special. Keep glass things low over a soft rug.

schedule.what: Draw Key A and Key B. Play with each key. Count the questions. Compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart of the average number of questions for each key.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the eight things. 2. Draw Key A on a big sheet. First question: 'Is it hard?' Hard things: steel spoon, wooden spoon, comb, bangle. Soft: rubber band, sock, hanky, candle. 3. Ask your child to add questions to each branch, until each thing is alone.
flow.say: We will build a key together. Our first question is: is it hard? That splits the eight things into four and four. Now let's add a question to each side.
flow.kid: Draw a branching key. First question: is it hard? Four things go left and four go right. Add questions until each thing is alone.
flow.parent: A good Key A looks like this. Hard: 'Is it made of metal or glass?' Yes gives steel spoon or bangle, split by 'Is it metal?'. No gives wooden spoon or comb, split by 'Is it wood?'. Soft: 'Is it cloth?' Yes gives sock or hanky, split by 'Is it wool?'. No gives rubber band or candle, split by 'Does it stretch?'.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Twenty Questions Race. You build a branching key, then play to find out how fast it is.

flow.do: Draw Key B on another sheet. It asks one question per thing. First ask if it is the steel spoon. If not, ask if it is the wooden spoon. If not, ask if it is the comb. Go on down the line.
flow.say: Key B is a different kind of key. Each question picks out just one thing. The line of questions is long.
flow.kid: Draw Key B. It asks about one thing at a time. Ask 'Is it the steel spoon?' If not, ask about the next. Keep going.

ask.q: Which key do you think will be faster?
good: Key A, because each question cuts the group in half.
Key B, because it might get lucky on the first question.

flow.do: 1. The other person picks a secret thing and does not say. 2. Your child uses Key A to find it and counts the questions. 3. Repeat until all eight things have been the secret thing. 4. Do the same with Key B. 5. Write the counts in the table.
flow.say: Pick a secret thing, and don't tell. I'll use Key A to find it, and count the questions. Then we do it with Key B.
flow.kid: Your helper picks a secret thing. Use Key A to find it. Count the questions. Do all eight things. Then do Key B.
flow.parent: With Key A every thing is found in exactly 3 questions. With Key B the counts are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 7. The last two things need 7 each. After 6 'no' answers only 2 are left, and one more question tells them apart.

flow.do: 1. Work out the average for each key: add all eight counts and divide by 8. 2. Draw the bar chart. 3. Compare with the guess.
flow.say: Let's find the average number of questions for each key. We add the eight counts together and divide by eight.
flow.kid: Add up the eight counts for each key. Divide by 8 to find the average. Draw a bar for each key.

check.q: Key A needed 3 questions for every thing. Key B needed 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 7. Which key is better for finding a thing when you do not know which it is?
options: Key A, because it takes the same short time for every thing
Key B, because it is quickest for the first thing
Neither, because they find the same things
check.why: Key A splits the group in half with every question, so it never needs more than 3. Key B is fastest only if the secret thing happens to be the first one. Picking Key B usually means counting the lucky best case and forgetting the unlucky worst case. Picking 'neither' mixes up finding the same things with finding them quickly.

chart.title: Made-up example results: average questions needed with each key
chart.note: With these eight things, Key A needs 3 questions each time. Key B needs 35 questions in total for all eight, which is about 4.4 each.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: You found every thing with both keys. Tell me three things. What do you think makes a key fast? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a question that splits the group in half makes the fastest key. What I saw: Key A needed 3 questions for every thing, but Key B needed up to 7. Why: each question that halves the group cuts the left over things in half again. Three halvings take eight things down to one.
flow.think: How many questions would a key like Key A need to find one thing among 16? Among 32?

experiments.context: In this experiment you draw two branching keys for the same eight things and play a guessing game with them. You count the questions each key needs, to find out which first question makes the fastest key.

experiments.title: Sort by Sound
experiments.question: Do things that look alike also sound alike? Is sorting by sound the same as sorting by looks?
experiments.predict: Before you test, line up your six things. Put the one you think will ring longest first and the shortest last. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Hold each thing so that almost nothing touches it. Hang spoons and the mug from a thread. Rest the katori, the tumbler and the foil container, open side up, on the tips of three fingers of a flat hand. Tap each one with the same pencil, in the same place, with the same light tap. Listen in a quiet room. Try each thing three times.

materials.item: six things: a steel katori, a steel tumbler, a steel spoon, an aluminium foil food container (the kind takeaway food comes in), a ceramic mug and a plastic spoon. If you have a brass or copper bowl, add it too.
strong thread, about as long as your arm
a pencil
a clock or phone with a stopwatch
the results table

experiments.safety: Tap lightly, especially on the ceramic mug. Do the test over a soft rug or a folded towel, in case something falls.

schedule.what: Sort by looks. Hang, tap and time each thing. Sort by sound. Compare the two sorts.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Make two lists of groups: one sorted by looks and one sorted by sound. Circle the things that moved to a different group.

flow.do: 1. Put the six things on a tray. 2. Ask your child to sort them by how they look: silver-coloured and not silver-coloured. 3. Write the groups in the table. 4. Ask them to guess which will ring longest, and why.
flow.say: Here are six things. First, sort them by how they look. Silver things in one group, and the rest in the other. Now guess which will ring longest when tapped. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Sort the six things by how they look. Write the groups. Now guess which will ring longest.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sort by Sound. You sort six things by how they look, and then by how they sound, to see if the groups match.

flow.do: 1. Tie a loop of thread round the handle of each spoon and the mug. Hold the other end so the thing hangs free. 2. Rest the katori, the tumbler and the foil container, open side up, on three fingertips of a flat hand. 3. Tap it lightly with a pencil and start timing. 4. Listen until you cannot hear it any more. 5. Write the seconds in the table. 6. Do it three times for each thing.
flow.say: Hold the thing so almost nothing touches it. Tap it once, gently. Listen. Count the seconds until the ring has completely faded.
flow.kid: Hang the spoon by its thread. Rest a bowl on your fingertips. Tap it once, lightly, with the pencil. Count how many seconds it rings. Write it down.
flow.parent: A hand wrapped round a thing stops the ringing, so hold it by a thread or on fingertips. It is quiet work, so turn off any fan or TV. Ring times are rough, and this is fine. Look at the differences, which are big. Try three times because one try may be a fluke. Expect the katori and the tumbler to ring for several seconds, and the foil container and plastic spoon hardly at all.

flow.do: 1. Make a new set of groups, by sound. For example, rings for a long time, rings for a short time, hardly rings. 2. Compare with the groups made by looks. 3. Circle any thing that moved to a different group.
flow.say: Now sort the same six things by how they sound. Do the groups look like the groups we made by sight?
flow.kid: Sort the six things again, by sound. Are the groups the same as before? Which thing moved?

check.q: Two bowls look the same. One rings for 8 seconds and one for 1 second. What can we say?
options: Sorting by looks hid a difference that sorting by sound showed
The bowls must be the same material
check.why: Looking alike does not mean sounding alike. The two bowls may be made of different materials, such as bell metal and brass. Sorting by sound found a difference that sorting by looks missed. Picking 'the same material' usually means the child trusts looks too much. A crack can also stop a bowl ringing, so check for one. But a crack is not the only reason.

chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: You sorted the same six things by looks and then by sound. Tell me three things. What do you think now about sorting by looks? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: sorting by sound gives different groups from sorting by looks. What I saw: the steel katori and the foil container were both silver, but the katori rang for 6 seconds and the container hardly rang. Why: the sound depends on the material and its shape and thickness, and looks do not show these. A bell-maker can sort scrap metal by ear for this reason, as in the story.
flow.think: When is it better to sort by looks? When is it better to sort by sound?

experiments.context: In this experiment you sort six things by how they look, then by how they sound. It shows that two things can look alike and sound different. It is the same trick as in this unit's story.

activities.title: Sort the Kitchen Drawer

materials.item: the cutlery drawer or a tray of kitchen tools (leave out knives and anything sharp)
sheets of paper for labels, a pencil

activities.safety: Sharp knives, peelers and graters stay out of the drawer for this game. A grown-up handles them.

schedule.what: Find the rule your family already uses. Sort the drawer two new ways.

activities.record: Write down the three rules you used. Draw one of your groupings.

flow.do: 1. Pull out the kitchen drawer. 2. Look at how things are arranged now. 3. Ask your child to work out the rule the family uses.
flow.say: Someone sorted this drawer long ago. There is a rule hiding in the way things are put away. Can you spot it?
flow.kid: Look at the drawer. How are things arranged? What rule do you think someone used?

ask.q: What is the rule for how things are put away?
good: Spoons together, forks together.
Things we use for eating are here, things for cooking are there.
Big things at the back, little things at the front.

flow.context: This is the first step of Sort the Kitchen Drawer. Every tidy drawer already has a sorting rule. You find it, and then try new ones.

flow.do: 1. Take everything out and put it on a table. 2. Sort by a new rule: what it is made of. 3. Mix and sort again: by what it is used for. 4. Take a photo of each sort.
flow.say: Now let's sort the whole drawer by a different rule. First, by what each thing is made of. Then, by what it is used for.
flow.kid: Take everything out. Sort it by material, such as steel, wood and plastic. Mix it up. Sort it again by use.
flow.parent: Notice which rule makes the drawer easier to use, and which makes it easier to clean. Both are good reasons. A steel spoon is in the steel group by material, and in the eating group by use.

flow.do: Put the things back by the rule that your child thinks works best. Ask why.
flow.say: Which rule do you want to put things back by? Why is it best?
flow.kid: Put the things back using the rule you like best. Why is it the best?
flow.think: Does the best rule depend on what you want to do? You might want to find a spoon fast, or clean the drawer.

activities.context: In this activity you find the sorting rule hiding in your kitchen drawer. Then you try two new rules.

activities.title: The Floor Venn

materials.item: two dupattas, saris or long ropes
ten things made of different materials, and two paper labels

activities.safety: Keep glass things low. Place them, do not throw them.

schedule.what: Make a Venn diagram on the floor. Sort ten things. Change one label and sort again.

activities.record: Draw your Venn diagram and write the names of the things in the right places.

flow.do: 1. Lay the two dupattas or hoops on the floor so that they overlap in the middle. 2. Label one circle 'Shiny' and the other 'Hard'. 3. Put the ten things in a heap.
flow.say: Here are two circles that overlap. One is for shiny things. One is for hard things. What do you think goes in the middle, where the circles overlap?
flow.kid: Make two overlapping circles on the floor. Label one Shiny. Label the other Hard. What goes in the middle?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Floor Venn. A Venn diagram uses two overlapping circles to sort things by two rules at once.

flow.do: 1. Pick up each thing. 2. Decide: shiny, hard, both or neither? 3. Place it in the right part. Both goes in the overlap. Neither goes outside both circles. 4. Count the things in each part.
flow.say: Pick up each thing and ask both questions. Is it shiny? Is it hard? Put it in the right place. If it is both, it goes in the middle.
flow.kid: Pick up each thing. Ask: is it shiny? Is it hard? Put it in the right place. Both goes in the middle. Neither goes outside.

ask.q: What does it mean to be in the middle? What about outside both circles?
good: In the middle it is both shiny and hard.
Outside it is neither shiny nor hard.

check.q: A rubber band is dull and bendy. In the Shiny and Hard Venn diagram, where does it go?
check.why: A dull, bendy rubber band is not shiny and not hard, so it fits neither rule. It goes outside both circles. Picking the overlap usually means it is seen as the place for odd things. It is really the place for things that fit both rules.

flow.do: Change one label, such as Hard to Metal. Ask your child to move the things to their new places.
flow.say: Now we change one label. The Hard circle becomes the Metal circle. Which things need to move?
flow.kid: Change one label. Hard becomes Metal. Which things need to move? Move them.
flow.think: Did the things change? Or only the rule?

activities.context: In this activity you make a Venn diagram on the floor. It has two overlapping circles, and you sort ten things by two rules.

activities.title: Dal Detective and the Sup

materials.item: a cup of clean dal or lentils
a pinch of rock salt crystals (khada namak) or a few tiny stones washed from a potted plant, mixed in by a grown-up
a spoonful of dry tea leaves, or dry curry leaves crushed into flakes
a flat tray, thali or sup, and a big sheet of newspaper

activities.safety: A grown-up mixes in the stones or salt. Work on a balcony or by an open window, with newspaper underneath. Do not cook this dal afterwards.

schedule.what: Pick out the stones by hand. Winnow the leaf flakes in a tray.

activities.record: Draw the three piles: dal, stones and leaf flakes. Write the rule used to make each pile.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up mixes the stones or salt crystals and the leaf flakes into the dal. 2. Spread the dal on a thali. 3. Ask your child to pick out the stones one at a time.
flow.say: In many homes, someone picks stones out of dal before cooking. That is sorting, and it has a rule. Is it dal, or is it not dal?
flow.kid: A grown-up mixes stones into the dal. Spread the dal on a plate. Pick out the stones. The rule is: dal or not dal?
flow.context: This is the first step of Dal Detective and the Sup. Cooks have sorted grains for centuries. You sort stones and light flakes out of dal, by hand and by wind.

flow.do: 1. Pour the dal and leaf flakes on a flat tray. 2. Hold the tray low, over newspaper, and gently toss the dal up about two centimetres, then catch it. 3. Blow gently across the tray while you toss. 4. Watch what happens to the light bits and the heavy bits.
flow.say: Farmers do this in a sup, a flat basket, to sort grain from husk. Our leaf flakes stand in for the husk. Toss gently. Blow across it. Watch what goes where.
flow.kid: Toss the dal gently in the tray, and blow across it. Watch the light bits float away. Watch the dal fall back.

ask.q: What does the blowing sort? What is the rule?
good: It sorts light from heavy.
Light bits blow away. Heavy dal falls back down.

check.q: In winnowing, why does the husk blow away but the grain stays?
options: The husk is lighter, so the wind moves it more
The wind blows only on the husk
The grain is stuck to the tray
check.why: The wind pushes on everything, but it moves a light thing much more than a heavy thing. So the light husk blows away while the heavy grain falls straight back. Picking 'the wind blows only on the husk' misses that the wind pushes the grain too. The weight of each thing decides how far it moves.

flow.do: Look at the three piles: dal, stones and leaf flakes. Ask how many rules were used.
flow.say: We made three piles with two different rules. What were the rules? Which rule used hands, and which used the wind?
flow.kid: Look at your three piles. How many rules did you use? Which rule used your hands? Which used the wind?
flow.think: People sorted grain by hand and with the wind for thousands of years. What tools do rice mills and flour mills use today?

activities.context: In this activity you sort stones and light flakes out of dal, as cooks and farmers have done for thousands of years. One rule uses your hands. The other uses the wind.

activities.title: Model Recycling Line

materials.item: a tray of mixed, clean bits: small scraps of paper, steel paper clips, plastic bottle caps, and a handful of dried rajma or chana, which stands in for glass
a fridge magnet or other magnet from home
a big bowl of water
three empty bowls and a towel

activities.safety: Keep the magnet away from phones and bank cards. Keep paper clips and small bits away from babies. Work over newspaper.

schedule.what: Plan the order of sorting steps. Run the line. Compare plans.

activities.record: Draw your recycling line in order. Write the rule at each step.

flow.do: 1. Tip the mixed bits on a tray. 2. Ask your child to plan the order of sorting steps. They may use blowing, a magnet and a bowl of water. 3. Write the plan.
flow.say: A recycling plant sorts in steps. Each step has one rule. You have three tools: your breath, a magnet and a bowl of water. In what order will you use them?
flow.kid: Plan your recycling line. You have three tools: breath, a magnet and water. Which comes first? Write down your plan.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Model Recycling Line. Real recycling plants sort mixed rubbish in steps, with one rule at each step. You copy this on a tray.

flow.do: 1. Blow gently over the tray to move the light paper into a bowl. 2. Run the magnet over the rest. The steel clips jump to it. Drop them in a bowl. 3. Tip what is left into the water. Scoop off what floats. 4. What sinks stays at the bottom. Dry it on a towel.
flow.say: Step one, blow away the lightest bits. Step two, the magnet picks up the steel. Step three, water: what floats and what sinks? Each step has its own rule.
flow.kid: Blow the paper away. Use the magnet on the clips. Put the rest in water. What floats? What sinks?
flow.parent: Expect paper to blow away and clips to jump to the magnet. Expect caps to float, and the rajma or chana to sink. A magnet attracts iron and most steel, but not aluminium, copper or plastic. If your fridge magnet is too weak to lift a clip, use any stronger magnet you have.

check.q: Why should the blowing step come before the water step?
options: Wet paper sticks to things and will not blow away
It does not matter which comes first
check.why: Once paper is wet, it clings to the tray and to other bits, so your breath cannot move it. So the dry step goes first. Picking 'it does not matter' usually means the order of steps was not thought about. In a real plant the order is chosen so each step can work.

flow.do: Compare the plan from step one with what you did. Ask what you would change.
flow.say: Did your plan work? If you did it again, would you change the order? Why?
flow.kid: Did your plan work? Would you change the order? Why?
flow.think: How would a real plant sort bottles made of different plastics? They look the same. What tool could tell them apart?

activities.context: In this activity you build a small recycling line on a tray. You sort a mix of rubbish in steps, using your breath, a magnet and water.

activities.title: Star Sorter: be Annie

materials.item: seven paper circles in colours blue, light blue, white, light yellow, yellow, orange and red, about the size of a coin
a marker and a long strip of paper

activities.safety: For the sky watch, go to a window, a balcony or a terrace with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Sort star circles from hottest to coolest. Look for a red star and a blue-white star in the night sky if you can.

activities.record: Draw a long strip with the seven colours in order. Write the letters O B A F G K M under them.

flow.do: 1. Mix up the seven coloured circles. 2. Say: a piece of iron in a fire glows red first. As it gets hotter, it glows yellow, then white. The hottest stars glow blue-white. 3. Ask your child to sort the circles from hottest to coolest star.
flow.say: Look at these seven stars. A blacksmith's iron glows red, then yellow, then white as it heats up. The hottest stars of all glow blue-white. Can you sort the stars from hottest to coolest?
flow.kid: Mix up the colour circles. Hot iron glows red, then yellow, then white. The hottest stars are blue-white. Sort the stars from hottest to coolest.

check.q: Which star is hotter on its surface, a blue star or a red star?
check.why: For stars, blue means hotter and red means cooler. Picking 'the red star' is very common, because red feels like fire. But a red-hot piece of iron can be heated more, until it glows yellow and then white. Stars hotter still glow blue-white.

flow.context: This is the first step of Star Sorter. Like Annie Jump Cannon, you sort stars into types, and then find out what the types mean.

flow.do: 1. Write letters under the colours. O is blue and B is light blue. A is white and F is light yellow. G is yellow, K is orange and M is red. 2. Show that the Sun is G. 3. Explain that Annie Jump Cannon sorted about 350,000 stars into these types.
flow.say: Annie Jump Cannon put the star types in order. She named them with seven letters: O, B, A, F, G, K and M. Our Sun is a G star. About how many stars did she sort? About 350,000. At her fastest, she sorted three stars in a minute.
flow.kid: Write O B A F G K M under the colours. Our Sun is a G star. Annie sorted about 350,000 stars!
flow.parent: Astronomers have long used a rhyme to remember the order, beginning 'Oh, Be A Fine...'. Your child can make up their own rhyme with the seven letters. For example: Our Baby Always Finds Great Kittens, Mostly.

ask.q: Where would a very hot star go on the strip? Where would a cool one go?
good: Hot on the blue end.
Cool on the red end.

flow.do: If the sky is clear, go outside or to a window with a grown-up after dark. Look for a reddish star and a blue-white star in Orion. Orion is easy to see in the evening sky from about December to March. Both stars are bright enough to see from a city.
flow.say: Orion is easy to find on winter evenings. Look for three stars in a row: that is Orion's belt. Above the belt is a red-orange star called Betelgeuse. Below it, on the other side, is a blue-white star called Rigel. Can you see the different colours?
flow.kid: Go out with a grown-up after dark. Find Orion. Look at the red star and the blue-white star. Can you see the colours?
flow.think: You are looking at light that left those stars hundreds of years ago. What else can colour tell us from far away?

activities.context: In this activity you sort seven coloured circles from hottest to coolest star, as Annie Jump Cannon sorted the stars into types.

activities.title: Which Circles Are You In?

materials.item: two ropes or dupattas for circles
family members or friends

activities.safety: Use only friendly rules about clothes, favourite things and what we like to do. Never sort people by their bodies, skin, religion, caste or how rich they are.

schedule.what: Play a living Venn diagram with your family. Then talk about belonging to many groups.

activities.record: Draw yourself in a Venn diagram of two circles you belong to. Write the names of the circles.

flow.do: 1. Lay two overlapping circles on the floor. 2. Label them with friendly rules, such as 'Wearing blue' and 'Likes mango'. 3. Explain that everyone will stand in the right place.
flow.say: Today we are the things being sorted. Let's use two friendly rules. Wearing something blue. And, likes mango. Where will you stand?
flow.kid: Make two circles on the floor. One is Wearing blue. One is Likes mango. Stand where you belong.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Circles Are You In? You become the things in a Venn diagram, using friendly rules.

flow.do: 1. Everyone stands where they belong. 2. Count people in each part. 3. Change one rule, such as 'Can ride a bicycle' and stand again. 4. Notice who moves.
flow.say: Stand where you belong. Who is in the middle? Who is outside both circles? Now change one rule. Who moves?
flow.kid: Stand where you belong. Count who is in the middle. Change one rule. Stand again. Who moved?

ask.q: Did you stay in the same place when we changed a rule? What does that tell us about groups?
good: No, I moved.
Everyone belongs to many groups.

flow.do: Sit and talk about belonging to many groups at once.
flow.say: You were in a different place for each rule. You belong to many groups at once. No one rule says who you are.
flow.kid: You were in a different place for each rule. You belong to lots of groups. No single rule says who you are.
flow.think: Why might it be unfair to sort people with just one rule?

activities.context: In this activity your family becomes a Venn diagram. You stand in circles for friendly rules, and find that everyone belongs to many groups at once.

activities.title: Oobleck: Solid or Liquid?

materials.item: two cups of cornflour
one cup of water
a big bowl and a spoon
newspaper or a big tray

activities.safety: Do not wash oobleck down the sink, because it can block the drain. Scrape it into a bin and wipe the bowl with paper first. It is safe to touch but not to eat.

schedule.what: Make oobleck. Test it slowly and fast. Decide which group it belongs to.

activities.record: Write down what it did when you moved slowly and when you hit it. Write which group you chose and why.

flow.do: 1. Put two cups of cornflour in the bowl. 2. Add the water a little at a time, mixing with your hand. 3. Stop when it feels thick but still runs when you tilt the bowl.
flow.say: This is called oobleck. The name comes from a Dr Seuss story. Mix slowly. We want it thick, but still able to drip.
flow.kid: Put cornflour in a bowl. Add water a little at a time. Mix with your hand. Stop when it is thick but drips.
flow.context: This is the first step of Oobleck: Solid or Liquid? You make a mix of cornflour and water that does not fit neatly into the solid group or the liquid group.

flow.do: 1. Move your fingers slowly through it. 2. Now punch it, or press it hard. 3. Scoop some up and roll it quickly in your hands. 4. Stop rolling and watch it.
flow.say: Poke it slowly. Now press it hard and fast. Roll it between your palms. Then stop. What does it do each time?
flow.kid: Poke it slowly. Punch it. Roll it in your hands. Then stop. What does it do each time?
flow.parent: Moved slowly, it flows like a liquid. Hit or squeezed fast, it feels hard like a solid. When you stop squeezing, the ball melts into your hand. Scientists call this a shear-thickening material. Give your child time to wonder at it.

ask.q: Is it a solid or a liquid?
good: Both.
It depends how fast I move it.
It is in the tricky middle.

flow.do: Compare oobleck with rice, ketchup and toothpaste. Ask where each belongs.
flow.say: Rice pours but is made of hard grains. Ketchup sits still and runs when shaken. Toothpaste holds its shape on the brush. Scientists made a new group for things like these.
flow.kid: Think of rice, ketchup and toothpaste. Scientists made a new group, called soft matter, for things like these.

check.q: Oobleck flows slowly and feels hard when hit. What is the best thing to say?
options: It does not fit solid or liquid neatly, so it is in the tricky middle
It must be a solid, because it can be hard
It must be a liquid, because it can flow
check.why: Oobleck acts like a solid when pushed fast and like a liquid when moved slowly. Both the 'must be solid' and 'must be liquid' answers pick one group and ignore what the other test shows. Scientists solve this by putting oobleck in a group called soft matter. It is a good example of the tricky middle.

flow.think: Scientists made a new group when old groups did not fit. When have you needed a new group?

activities.context: In this activity you make oobleck from cornflour and water. It acts like a liquid and a solid. It is a great example of a tricky middle.

projects.title: Our Home Materials Museum

materials.item: fifteen small things from around the house, each made of one material
an egg tray or a few small boxes for displays
paper, scissors, tape and markers
a phone camera to zoom in, or a magnifying glass if you have one

projects.safety: Choose things that are safe to handle. Keep sharp things out.

schedule.what: Collect fifteen things. Sort them three ways and label the displays.
Choose ten things. Build a branching key to find each one. Test it yourself.
Open the museum to visitors. Let them use the key. Fix what confused them.

projects.record: Photograph the three sorts. Keep the drawing of the branching key. Write down two things your visitors found confusing and how you fixed them.

flow.do: 1. Walk round the house and collect fifteen small things, each made of one material. 2. Put them on a table. 3. Make a label for each one.
flow.say: We are going to make a small museum of materials. A museum is a place where things are collected, sorted and shown. First, collect fifteen things.
flow.kid: Collect fifteen small things from around the house. Each should be made of one material. Make a label for each.
flow.context: This is the first step of Our Home Materials Museum. Over three days you build a small museum. You sort fifteen things, build a branching key for ten of them, and test it on visitors.

flow.do: 1. Sort the fifteen things into groups by material and display each group in an egg tray cup or box. 2. Sort them again by a property, such as hard or soft. 3. Sort them again by a rule of your own. 4. Photograph each display and write the rule on a card.
flow.say: A good museum shows the same things in different ways. Sort by material first. Then by a property. Then by a rule you invent.
flow.kid: Sort your fifteen things three ways. Show each sort in a tray or box. Photograph it. Write the rule on a card.

ask.q: Which of your three sorts would a visitor like best? Why?
good: The one with the clearest rule.
The one with the most surprising groups.

flow.do: 1. Choose ten things for the key. 2. Draw a first question that splits them roughly in half. 3. Add a question on each branch until each thing is alone. 4. Test your key by choosing a thing secretly and following the key.
flow.say: Now we make a branching key for ten of our things. The first question should split them in half. Then keep splitting until every thing is alone.
flow.kid: Choose ten things. Draw a key with yes or no questions. Split them in half each time. Test it yourself.
flow.parent: Good questions have a clear answer and can be tested by anyone. If the key has a branch with a very long chain, try a different first question. Ten things need at least four questions, because three questions can only tell eight things apart.

flow.do: Leave the museum and key ready. Tomorrow, visitors will try them.
flow.say: Our museum is ready. Tomorrow, we open the doors.
flow.kid: Your museum is ready. Tomorrow, you open the doors.
flow.wait: Leave everything ready for the next day.

flow.do: 1. Invite two visitors, such as family or neighbours. 2. Each picks a secret thing and uses your key to find it. 3. Watch quietly. Write down any question that confused them. 4. Fix the key.
flow.say: Welcome, visitors. Please pick a secret thing and use our key to find it. We will watch and learn what to fix.
flow.kid: Invite two visitors. They pick a secret thing and use your key. Watch quietly. Note what confuses them.
flow.think: What did you learn from watching your visitors use your key?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences about what they learned. Then fix the key and put the museum on display.
flow.say: Our visitors have used the key. Tell me three things. What do you think makes a good key? What did you see that shows it? And why?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why. Then fix your key.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a good key has clear questions that anyone can answer the same way. What I saw: my visitor got stuck on 'Is it pretty?', so I changed it to 'Is it shiny?'. Why I changed it: a clear rule gives the same answer for everyone.

projects.context: In this three-day project you build a small museum of materials in your home. You sort fifteen things three ways, build a branching key, and test it on visitors.

challenges.title: Clean the Mixed-Up Jar
challenges.problem: A jar holds rice, steel paper clips, dried rajma, plastic beads and dry crushed leaves, all mixed together. Your job is to separate it into five clean piles, using as few steps as you can.
constraints: You may not pick every bit out by hand one at a time.
You may only use things you find at home.
Time each way you try, and count the steps.
materials: a jar of the mixed bits, made by a grown-up (use beads bigger than a rice grain)
a magnet, a colander or sieve, a bowl of water, a tray and a clock
general: Use a magnet to take out the steel paper clips.
Use a sieve or colander with holes the right size, so small bits fall through and big bits stay.
Blow gently over the tray, or toss it in a flat tray, to take out the light leaves.
Put what is left into water. Some plastic beads float and some sink, so test one first. Rajma sinks.
creative: Tilt a tray and tap it gently. Round beads roll away faster than rice grains.
Rub a plastic comb on dry hair, then hold it over the tray. It may pick up the light leaf bits.
Stack two sieves with different hole sizes. Pour through both to make three piles in one go.
Think of a sorting machine in a factory. What is the clever step that you could copy?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own order of steps. Draw it, try it, and time it. Is your line faster than the others?

flow.do: 1. Look at the mixed jar. 2. Ask your child to list the five kinds of thing. 3. Ask which tool might work on each.
flow.say: Here is a jar with five kinds of thing all mixed together. For each kind, which tool might take it out? A magnet? A sieve? Your breath? Water?
flow.kid: Look at the jar. Name the five kinds of things. For each one, which tool might take it out?
flow.context: This is the first step of Clean the Mixed-Up Jar. This is an engineering challenge. You must separate a jar of mixed things into clean piles, in as few steps as you can.

flow.do: Before trying anything, draw a plan of the steps, in order.
flow.say: Before we try anything, let's think like engineers. Draw your plan. Which comes first, second and third?
flow.kid: Think like an engineer. Draw your plan. What comes first? What comes next?

flow.do: 1. Try the plan. 2. Time it. 3. Count the steps. 4. Try one change and time it again.
flow.say: Try your plan and time it. Then change one thing and try again. Which version is faster?
flow.kid: Try your plan. Time it. Change one thing. Try again. Which is faster?
flow.parent: A magnet first is usually best. Then blow or toss for the leaves. Then shake the rest in a colander or a sieve with big holes: rice falls through, and the rajma and beads stay. If the rice will not pass, tilt the tray and tap it, so the round beads roll away. Pick out the rajma, or try water if your beads float. If a step does not work, look for one property where the two kinds differ, such as size, weight or floating, and use a tool that sorts by it.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together. Then invent a new one.
flow.say: Here is what engineers usually do, and some creative ideas. Can you invent something new?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ways and the creative ideas. Now invent your own. Can you beat them?
flow.think: Every step in a sorting line asks one question about one property. What is the cleverest question you used?

challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You separate a jar of five mixed things into clean piles, using as few steps as possible.

challenges.title: A Key for Everyone
challenges.problem: Many people cannot use a key that depends on reading. Design a branching key for ten things. A young child who cannot read, or a person who is blind, must be able to use it.
constraints: The key must use no written words, or only a few.
Every question must have a yes or no answer.
You must test it on a real person who did not help to make it.
materials: a younger child or a family member who will help test
general: Draw a large clear picture for each question.
Use a green tick for yes and a red cross for no.
Put one question on each page and turn the page for yes or no.
creative: Make a key you can feel. Questions such as 'Is it rough?' or 'Is it cold?' use touch instead of sight.
Use sound. Tap each thing. 'Does it ring?' is a question a blind person can answer.
Use colour and shape symbols that match the questions, so that a child learns the symbols as they go.
Make a key in another language that your family speaks, and ask a grandparent to check it.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Draw it, make it, and test it on someone. What did they find easy? What confused them?

flow.do: 1. Choose ten things for the key. 2. Think about who will use it. 3. List the questions you can ask without reading.
flow.say: A good key works for the person using it. Who will use ours? What can they do that helps? Look, touch, listen, smell?
flow.kid: Choose ten things. Think about who will use your key. What can they do? See? Touch? Hear?
flow.context: This is the first step of A Key for Everyone. This is a design challenge. You make a branching key that works even if the user cannot read, or cannot see.

flow.do: 1. Write the questions on paper. 2. Draw a picture or a symbol for each one. 3. Build the key as a chain of pages, or as a tree.
flow.say: Now draw the questions as pictures or symbols. A green tick for yes. A red cross for no. One question on each page.
flow.kid: Draw each question as a picture. Use a tick for yes and a cross for no. Make your key, page by page.
flow.parent: Think about the first question carefully. It should split the ten things roughly in half. If you want a key that can be felt, use cardboard shapes with different textures for yes and no.

flow.do: 1. Ask your tester to find a secret thing using the key. 2. Do not help. 3. Write down what confuses them. 4. Fix it.
flow.say: Please find the thing I hide, using only our key. I will not help. I will watch and learn.
flow.kid: Ask someone to use your key. Do not help them. Watch carefully. What confuses them? Fix it.

flow.do: Compare your key with the usual solutions and the creative ideas.
flow.say: Which of the ideas would you try next? Who else could use a key like this?
flow.kid: Which idea would you try next? Who else could use your key?
flow.think: When we design for someone else, what do they need that we do not? Who gets left out when a rule only works for people who read?

challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make a branching key for ten things. A child who cannot read, or a person who cannot see, can use it.

opts: A question that every thing can answer, to decide its group
quiz.why: A rule is a question, like 'Is it shiny?'. Each thing is checked against it. Picking 'the name of a group' mixes up the question and its answer.

quiz.p: Which is the best sorting rule?
quiz.why: 'Is it shiny?' has a clear answer that anyone can check. 'Pretty' and 'nice' depend on who is asked.

quiz.p: A brick is hard and dull. We sort by hard or soft, then by shiny or dull. What happens to the brick?
opts: It goes in the hard group, then in the dull group
It goes in the hard group both times
It goes in the soft group
quiz.why: The same brick lands in a different named group each time, because each rule asks a different question. Picking 'hard both times' usually means the second rule was ignored.

quiz.p: Why can one thing be in many groups?
opts: Each rule asks a different question about it
quiz.why: A steel spoon is shiny, hard and metal. Each is a different question. The spoon does not change. Picking 'the thing changes' is a common idea, but only the rule changes.

quiz.p: A candle is hard, but a fingernail can mark it. What is the best way to settle where it goes?
opts: Use a fair test, and let the test decide
quiz.why: A test gives the same answer for everyone. Guessing can differ from person to person. Throwing it away leaves the problem unsolved.

quiz.p: Which of these is a good way to deal with a tricky middle thing?
quiz.why: A middle group gives honest room to a thing that is truly between. Hiding or pretending makes the sort less true.

quiz.p: In a Venn diagram of Shiny and Hard, where does a glass bangle go?
quiz.why: A glass bangle is shiny and hard, so it fits both rules and goes in the overlap. Picking 'outside' means one rule was missed.

quiz.p: In the Carroll table, what do the four boxes show?
opts: Both, only the first, only the second, and neither
quiz.why: Two yes or no rules make four combinations. Each thing goes in exactly one box.
quiz.context: A Carroll table sorts things by two yes or no rules at once, using four boxes.

quiz.p: A key has three questions in a row, each splitting the group in half. How many things can it tell apart?
quiz.why: Each question doubles the number of branches: 2, then 4, then 8. Picking 6 or 3 usually means adding instead of doubling.
quiz.context: A branching key asks yes or no questions. A good question splits the group in half.

quiz.p: Which first question makes the fastest key for eight things, four hard and four soft?
quiz.why: 'Is it hard?' splits the eight things four and four. Asking about one thing at a time is slow.

quiz.p: A kabadiwala keeps paper, glass and iron in separate piles. Why?
opts: Each material is recycled in its own way
quiz.why: The sort has a job: selling to different buyers. Picking 'it looks tidy' misses the purpose.

quiz.p: Winnowing sorts grain from husk. Which rule does the wind use?
quiz.why: The wind moves light husk more than heavy grain. Picking 'colour' is a common guess, but colour does not change how hard the wind pushes.

quiz.p: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his table?
opts: He expected undiscovered elements to fill them
quiz.why: The pattern pointed to elements nobody had found. Three of them, gallium, scandium and germanium, were found and matched his predictions.

quiz.p: What do the star letters O, B, A, F, G, K, M show?
opts: How hot the surface of the star is
quiz.why: Annie Jump Cannon sorted the stars into these types by their light, and Cecilia Payne showed that the types tell temperature. Picking 'how far' is a common guess, but the letters here tell heat.

quiz.p: Which star is hotter on its surface?
quiz.why: For stars, blue means hotter. Picking red is very common because we link red with fire.

quiz.p: Do scientists agree on exactly what a species is?
opts: No, there are over twenty different definitions
Yes, there is only one rule
quiz.why: Biologists still argue. Different definitions work better for animals, plants and bacteria.

quiz.p: Why was Pluto moved to a new group in 2006?
opts: Astronomers changed the rule for what a planet is
quiz.why: The rule changed, not Pluto. Some astronomers still disagree with the new rule. Picking 'Pluto got smaller' is a common guess, but Pluto did not change.

quiz.p: Dan Shechtman found a pattern that scientists thought was impossible. What happened to the definition of a crystal?
quiz.why: Other scientists checked his work, and the boxes were changed to fit what was found. Picking 'stayed the same' ignores that science can correct itself.

quiz.p: Why do ketchup and cornflour mixed with water belong to the tricky middle?
opts: They act like a solid and like a liquid
They are too small to see
quiz.why: Both change with how fast you move them. Scientists put such things in a group called soft matter.

applications: Libraries put books on shelves by subject, so that you can find the one you want.
Post offices sort letters by PIN code, in layers like a branching key. The first digit gives the region, the next ones narrow it down to one post office.
Recycling plants sort rubbish with magnets, wind, water, cameras and jets of air.
Doctors use branching charts of yes or no questions to work out what illness a patient has.
Bird and plant books have keys. You answer questions about the beak or the leaf, and the key tells you the name.
The periodic table guides chemists, who use its columns to guess how a new material will behave.
Astronomers use star types to tell how hot a star is and how long it will live.
Computers sort millions of names or numbers in a blink, using sorting methods that follow clear rules.
Online shops let you filter by colour, size and price. Each filter is a sorting rule.
Tea estates grade tea leaves by size, and mango sellers in a mandi sort mangoes by size and ripeness.
Farmers winnow grain, and flour mills use sieves to sort flour by how fine it is.
Geologists test how hard a mineral is by seeing what scratches it, using the Mohs scale.
Hospitals triage patients, which means sorting them by how urgently they need help.
Search engines and AI programs sort pictures and words, and need to be tested to be fair to everyone.

open_questions.why_open: Biologists have written over twenty different definitions. No single rule works for bacteria, plants and animals.

open_questions.q: How do piles of grains and sand really flow?
open_questions.why_open: A pile of sand acts like a solid, a liquid or a gas, depending on how you treat it. Scientists do not yet have one complete theory for this.

open_questions.q: What exactly is glass, and why does a liquid turn into glass as it cools?
open_questions.why_open: Glass has no pattern like a crystal and does not flow like a liquid. In 1995 the physicist Philip Anderson wrote that glass might be the deepest unsolved problem in solid state physics.

open_questions.q: How many elements can there be? Can element 119 be made?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists make heavy elements in laboratories, but each one lasts for a tiny fraction of a second. Some think there could be more stable ones, but nobody knows.

open_questions.q: Are there more 'impossible' materials that fit none of our groups?
open_questions.why_open: Quasicrystals were found by accident. Scientists keep making new materials, and some may need new groups.

open_questions.q: How does the brain make groups so fast, even in tiny babies?
open_questions.why_open: Babies sort cats from dogs after seeing only a few. Brain scientists are still working out how the brain does it.

open_questions.q: Are groups found in nature, or made by us?
open_questions.why_open: Some groups, like gold, seem natural. Others depend on our needs. Philosophers and scientists still disagree.

open_questions.q: Can computers sort fairly for everyone?
open_questions.why_open: Programs learn from examples we give them. Making sure the examples are fair is very hard, and researchers are still learning how.
