maths.problem: In the experiment One Heap, Three Rules, a child sorted twelve things into the four boxes of a Carroll table. The chart shows how many things were in each box. How many things were soft, and how many were dull?
maths.answer: 6 things were soft and 8 were dull.
maths.explain: Soft things are in two boxes: soft and shiny has 1, and soft and dull has 5. 1 + 5 = 6. Dull things are also in two boxes: hard and dull has 3, and soft and dull has 5. 3 + 5 = 8. Check: 6 soft and 6 hard make 12, and 4 shiny and 8 dull make 12.
maths.context: In the experiment One Heap, Three Rules, you sort twelve things by hard or soft, then by shiny or dull. Each thing goes in one of four boxes. These are made-up results.

chart.title: How many things in each box of the Carroll table (made-up)

maths.why_maths: When you sort, you count. Adding the right boxes answers questions about a whole group, such as how many were soft.

maths.problem: In the Floor Venn, ten things were sorted. 5 were shiny. 4 were hard. 2 were both shiny and hard. How many things were neither shiny nor hard?
maths.explain: The 2 things that are both were counted once in the shiny 5 and again in the hard 4. So the things that are shiny or hard are 5 + 4 - 2 = 7. The other things are 10 - 7 = 3. Check with the diagram: only shiny 3, both 2, only hard 2, neither 3. That makes 3 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 10.
maths.context: In the Floor Venn activity, you make two overlapping circles, one for shiny and one for hard. Things that fit both rules go in the overlap. These are made-up numbers.

answer_chart.title: The ten things in a Venn diagram (made-up)

maths.why_maths: Things in the overlap fit two rules, so they are easy to count twice by mistake. A Venn diagram shows the problem, and the subtraction fixes it.

maths.problem: Each good question doubles the number of things a branching key can tell apart. One question tells 2 apart. Two questions tell 4 apart. Three tell 8 apart. How many things can five questions tell apart? And how many questions are needed to tell 16 things apart?
maths.answer: Five questions tell 32 things apart. To tell 16 things apart you need 4 questions.
maths.explain: Keep doubling. 2, 4, 8, then 16 for four questions, then 32 for five. So five questions tell 32 things apart. The number 16 comes after four doublings, so 16 things need 4 questions.
maths.context: In the Twenty Questions Race, you build a branching key. A good key splits the group in half with every question. So the number of things it can tell apart doubles.

answer_chart.title: Questions asked and things told apart

maths.why_maths: A number pattern lets you see ahead. Once you know that each question doubles the number, you can work out the answer for any number of questions.

maths.problem: In Sort by Sound, a steel katori rang for 6 seconds and a steel tumbler for 5 seconds. A steel spoon rang for 2 seconds and a ceramic mug for 1 second. Draw a bar chart. How many seconds longer did the steel katori ring than the steel spoon? Both are made of steel, so why might they ring for different times?
maths.answer: 4 seconds longer. They are the same material, so the difference must come from their shape and size.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each thing, as tall as its number of seconds. The katori bar reaches 6. The spoon bar reaches 2. 6 - 2 = 4. So the katori rang 4 seconds longer. The material is the same, so something else changed the sound: the katori is a wide, thin bowl, and the spoon is a small, thick strip.
maths.context: In the experiment Sort by Sound, you hang or rest things so they can ring, and tap them lightly. You time how long they ring. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: After a test you have a list of numbers. A bar chart makes the longest and shortest ringers jump out, and taking one number from another shows the gap.

maths.problem: A kabadiwala sorts a heap into piles. There are 12 kilograms of paper, 7 kilograms of iron, 5 kilograms of plastic and 4 kilograms of glass. How many kilograms are in the whole heap?
maths.explain: Add the four piles. 12 + 7 = 19. 19 + 5 = 24. 24 + 4 = 28. Check by adding in a different order. 12 + 4 = 16, and 7 + 5 = 12, and 16 + 12 = 28.
maths.context: A kabadiwala sorts old things into piles, one for each material, and weighs each pile before paying. These are made-up numbers.
maths.why_maths: A sorted heap is easier to count. Adding the piles gives the total weight, which is what a kabadiwala needs to know to pay the right price.

maths.problem: Mendeleev published his table in 1869. Germanium, one of the elements he predicted, was found in 1886. How many years later was germanium found?
maths.explain: Find the gap between 1869 and 1886. 1886 - 1869 = 17. You can count up. From 1869 to 1880 is 11 years, and from 1880 to 1886 is 6 more. 11 + 6 = 17.
maths.context: Mendeleev left gaps in his table in 1869 and predicted that new elements would fill them. Gallium was found in 1875, scandium in 1879 and germanium in 1886.
maths.why_maths: A prediction is only strong if we know how long it took to come true. Subtracting the years tells us how long scientists waited.

how_we_found_out.story: For most of the 1900s, scientists sorted every solid with ordered atoms into one group: crystals. A crystal's atoms sit in a pattern that repeats, like tiles on a floor. Mathematicians had shown that a repeating pattern can never have five-fold symmetry, the kind of balance a five-pointed star has. So everyone believed that an ordered solid with five-fold symmetry could not exist. On 8 April 1982, Dan Shechtman, an Israeli scientist working in the United States, cooled a melted mix of aluminium and manganese very fast. He looked at it with an electron microscope. The spots in his picture had ten-fold symmetry, which only an ordered pattern with five-fold symmetry could make. He wrote 'ten-fold???' in his notebook. Many scientists said he had made a mistake, and Linus Pauling, a famous chemist, argued against him for years. But other laboratories made the same material and saw the same pattern. In 1992 the International Union of Crystallography changed its definition of a crystal. Shechtman won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2011.
how_we_found_out.who: Dan Shechtman (1982), with Ilan Blech, Denis Gratias and John Cahn, who published the result with him in 1984
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That every solid with ordered atoms has a pattern that repeats. Shechtman's metal had an ordered pattern with five-fold symmetry, which no repeating pattern can have. Other laboratories made it too, so the rule for what counts as a crystal had to change.
how_we_found_out.art: A scientist at an electron microscope in a 1980s laboratory, looking at a picture of spots arranged in a ten-pointed ring, with a notebook open beside him.
